title: Breaking Scale Separation in Metamaterials' homogenization: Interface-Inertia-Enhanced Relaxed Micromorphic Model
summary: Homogenized continuum models are widely used to describe wave propagation and band-gap behavior in mechanical metamaterials without explicitly resolving their microstructure. Their validity, however, typically relies on the classical separation of scales assumption, according to which the wavelength of the propagating disturbance is much larger than the characteristic size of the unit cell. In finite-size metamaterial samples and at higher frequencies, this assumption progressively breaks down, and the dynamic response becomes strongly influenced by the way the microstructure is truncated at the external boundaries. In this work we introduce a fundamentally new concept in the homogenized description of mechanical metamaterials: the inertial contribution of macroscopic interfaces. We show that different truncations of the same lattice generate boundaries with distinct mass distributions, which lead to measurable differences in the dynamic response of finite-sized specimens. To capture this complex mechanism in a homogenized framework, we extend the relaxed micromorphic model by introducing a kinetic surface energy defined on the boundary of the considered body. This generates an additional inertial term in the boundary conditions that can be seen as the homogenized counterpart of the interface inertia produced by the truncation of the microstructure. As a result, the homogenized model can now distinguish between finite-sized specimens that share identical bulk properties but differ only in the configuration of their interfaces. The proposed formulation preserves the variational structure of the relaxed micromorphic model while enabling the continuum to reproduce boundary-dependent responses observed in fully resolved simulations, particularly in frequency regimes ....... See the PDF for the full abstract.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new concept in homogenized modeling of mechanical metamaterials by adding inertial contributions from macroscopic interfaces. The authors extend the relaxed micromorphic model with a kinetic surface energy on boundaries, allowing the continuum model to distinguish between finite specimens with identical bulk properties but different interface configurations—capturing boundary-dependent dynamic responses that standard homogenization misses.
AI.motivation: Classical homogenized continuum models for mechanical metamaterials rely on the separation of scales assumption (wavelength >> unit cell size). In finite samples and at higher frequencies, this assumption fails, and the dynamic response depends on how the microstructure is truncated at boundaries. Existing homogenized models cannot capture these boundary-dependent effects.
AI.method: The authors extend the relaxed micromorphic model by introducing a kinetic surface energy defined on the boundary of the body. This adds an inertial term to the boundary conditions, serving as the homogenized counterpart of interface inertia produced by microstructure truncation. The formulation preserves the variational structure of the relaxed micromorphic model.
AI.result: The homogenized model can distinguish between finite-sized specimens that share identical bulk properties but differ only in interface configuration. It reproduces boundary-dependent responses observed in fully resolved simulations, particularly in frequency regimes where classical homogenization fails.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formulation enables continuum models to capture interface-inertia effects in finite metamaterial samples, overcoming a key limitation of classical homogenization at higher frequencies and with finite-size effects.

title: Exact Total Variation Minimizers as Non-Oscillatory Limiters in High-Order Methods for Conservation Laws
summary: High-order numerical methods for conservation laws can generate spurious oscillations near discontinuities. We propose to suppress these oscillations by post-processing the numerical solution with a total variation (TV) denoising step that reduces the total variation of the nodal values. For a general analysis operator, the resulting discrete minimization problem need not satisfy the submodularity property that existing exact max-flow algorithms require, so we instead compute the TV minimizer exactly using a differential inclusion algorithm. In one dimension, the differential inclusion algorithm computes the TV minimizer in finitely many steps, requires no tuning of algorithmic parameters, and preserves the total mass. In two dimensions, we apply the 1D algorithm dimension by dimension. We test the method as a post-processing limiter for Fourier pseudospectral methods and a fifth-order finite difference scheme applied to scalar conservation laws, compressible Euler equations, and the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a TV denoising post-processing step to suppress spurious oscillations in high-order numerical methods for conservation laws. Since the discrete minimization problem lacks submodularity for general analysis operators, they use a differential inclusion algorithm that computes the TV minimizer exactly—in finitely many steps in 1D with no tuning parameters and mass preservation, applied dimension-by-dimension in 2D. The method is tested as a limiter for pseudospectral and finite difference schemes across scalar and compressible/incompressible Euler equations.
AI.motivation: High-order numerical methods for conservation laws suffer from spurious oscillations near discontinuities, which need to be suppressed to maintain solution quality.
AI.method: Post-process the numerical solution with a TV denoising step. Instead of max-flow algorithms (which require submodularity not satisfied here), use a differential inclusion algorithm that computes the TV minimizer exactly. Apply the 1D algorithm dimension-by-dimension in 2D.
AI.result: The differential inclusion algorithm computes the TV minimizer in finitely many steps in 1D, requires no parameter tuning, and preserves total mass. Tests show effectiveness as a post-processing limiter for Fourier pseudospectral methods and a fifth-order finite difference scheme on scalar conservation laws, compressible Euler, and 2D incompressible Euler equations.
AI.conclusion: TV denoising via differential inclusion offers an exact, parameter-free approach to suppressing oscillations in high-order methods while preserving key physical properties like mass.

title: Dynamical Low-Rank Filters for Data Assimilation
summary: We propose dynamical low-rank (DLR) type filters for data-assimilation problems based on stochastic differential equations (SDEs). In detail, first we derive a DLRA filter for minimizing jointly the mean and covariance error, as well as a strategy to efficiently include the relevant orthogonal directions. This last approach allows the main subspace to evolve also according to the observation operator. Those procedures naturally extend to a Kalman-Bucy type filter when dealing with linear drift, and to ensemble methods, too, resulting also suitable for problems described by nonlinear drift and possible non-Gaussian distribution. Moreover, we further propose a preliminary particle-type DLRA filter that shows potentiality in nonlinear settings. Numerical simulations show the efficacy of these procedures in relevant applications, opening up to further studies in these filtering directions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes dynamical low-rank (DLR) type filters for data assimilation in stochastic differential equations (SDEs), including a DLRA filter that jointly minimizes mean and covariance error, strategies to incorporate observation-operator-driven orthogonal directions, extensions to Kalman-Bucy and ensemble methods for nonlinear/non-Gaussian settings, and a preliminary particle-type DLRA filter. Numerical simulations demonstrate efficacy.
AI.motivation: To develop efficient filtering methods for data assimilation in SDEs that handle high-dimensional problems by exploiting low-rank structure, while addressing both mean and covariance errors and accommodating nonlinear and non-Gaussian settings.
AI.method: Derives DLR-type filters including: (1) a DLRA filter jointly minimizing mean and covariance error, (2) a strategy for efficiently incorporating relevant orthogonal directions so the main subspace evolves with the observation operator, (3) extensions to Kalman-Bucy filters for linear drift, (4) ensemble methods for nonlinear drift and non-Gaussian distributions, and (5) a preliminary particle-type DLRA filter for nonlinear settings.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed procedures in relevant applications, showing potential for further studies in these filtering directions.
AI.conclusion: The DLR-based filtering framework provides a versatile and promising approach for data assimilation in SDEs, applicable across linear and nonlinear settings, with particle-type extensions showing potential for future research.

title: Comparison of a Parametric Physics-Informed Neural Network and a Tensorial Reduced-Order Model for the Shallow-Water Dam-Break Problem
summary: We develop two parametric data-driven reduced models: a physics-informed neural network (PINN) and a non-intrusive tensorial reduced-order model (TROM), and apply both approaches to the parametrized one-dimensional shallow-water dam-break problem. Both reduced models do not require time integration and learn a direct solution map from space, time, and dam-break parameters to the physical state. We present a detailed comparison for out-of-sample and extrapolated parameter values. In addition, we demonstrate that it is essential to introduce shock-aware collocation to improve the robustness of the PINN model.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and compares two parametric data-driven reduced models (PINN and non-intrusive TROM) for the 1D shallow-water dam-break problem, both learning direct solution maps without time integration, with shock-aware collocation improving PINN robustness.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of efficiently and accurately modeling parametrized shallow-water dam-break problems, which involve shocks and discontinuities, by developing data-driven reduced models that avoid time integration and provide fast direct solution mapping.
AI.method: Two non-intrusive data-driven approaches are developed: (1) a physics-informed neural network (PINN) and (2) a non-intrusive tensorial reduced-order model (TROM). Both learn a direct mapping from space, time, and dam-break parameters to the physical state without requiring time integration. Shock-aware collocation is introduced to enhance PINN robustness.
AI.result: Detailed comparisons are presented for out-of-sample and extrapolated parameter values, demonstrating the performance of both models and showing that shock-aware collocation is essential for improving PINN robustness.
AI.conclusion: Both PINN and TROM are viable data-driven reduced models for the dam-break problem, but shock-aware collocation is critical for making the PINN approach robust in handling shock discontinuities.

title: LoKI-GM: a global model framework for plasma chemistry studies
comment: Submitted to Plasma Sources Science and Technology
summary: Global (zero-dimensional or spatially averaged) models are widely employed to study complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas (LTPs). By adopting a spatially average description of the plasma, they substantially reduce the computational cost while still providing reliable and detailed insight into the key processes taking place in the plasma. In their most general formulation, global models involve the coupled solution of a Boltzmann solver (to describe the electron kinetics) and a Chemistry solver (to describe the heavy-species kinetics). This paper presents a tutorial on the LisbOn Kinetics Global Model (LoKI-GM) framework, developed in MATLAB and available as open-source code. The framework couples the Boltzmann solver LoKI-B, which solves the space-independent form of the two-term electron Boltzmann equation for non-magnetised non-equilibrium LTPs, excited by DC/HF electric fields or time-dependent (non-oscillatory) electric fields, and the Chemistry solver LoKI-C, which solves the system of zero-dimensional rate balance equations for the main charged and neutral species in the plasma and at the surface, receiving as input the kinetic schemes for the gas/plasma/surface system under study. The inclusion of several transport models together with support for surface kinetics models are distinguishing features of LoKI-GM compared with other global chemistry models. We briefly present the formulation of LoKI-GM, including its numerical solution strategy, input/output parameters, and calculation workflow for both active discharges and afterglow plasmas. The main differences with respect to existing global models are highlighted, and the flexibility of the code for plasma chemistry studies is demonstrated through representative simulation results obtained across a range of gas discharge configurations and operating conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a tutorial on LoKI-GM, an open-source MATLAB framework that couples the Boltzmann solver LoKI-B with the chemistry solver LoKI-C to perform global (zero-dimensional) modeling of low-temperature plasmas, featuring multiple transport models and support for surface kinetics.
AI.motivation: Global models are widely used to study complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas due to their computational efficiency, but there is a need for a flexible open-source framework that integrates both electron kinetics (Boltzmann solver) and heavy-species chemistry in a unified manner.
AI.method: LoKI-GM couples two solvers: LoKI-B, which solves the two-term electron Boltzmann equation for non-magnetised non-equilibrium LTPs under DC/HF or time-dependent electric fields, and LoKI-C, which solves zero-dimensional rate balance equations for charged and neutral species in the plasma and at the surface. The framework includes multiple transport models and supports surface kinetics models.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates the flexibility of LoKI-GM through representative simulation results across a range of gas discharge configurations and operating conditions, highlighting its distinguishing features compared to existing global chemistry models, particularly its transport models and surface kinetics support.
AI.conclusion: LoKI-GM provides a flexible, open-source global model framework for plasma chemistry studies, capable of modeling both active discharges and afterglow plasmas, with numerical solution strategy and calculation workflow presented for users.

title: Performance Benchmarking: Software for the Density Matrix Renormalization Group
summary: The performance of scientific software often determines the scale of problems that can be solved in practice. As multiple implementations of the same algorithm emerge, systematic evaluation is needed to compare their strengths and limitations. The density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm, widely used to study quantum systems, has over 50 software implementations. These implementations vary in multiple aspects that can strongly affect performance. However, despite the need, performance evaluations of these implementations are scarce and lack a consistent standard; many existing evaluations are either too incomplete to enable meaningful comparisons or focus on objectives other than direct performance comparisons, thereby limiting understanding of how the implementations compare. Here, we present a performance-oriented benchmarking framework to facilitate meaningful comparisons of DMRG implementations, and we apply it to quantify the performance of eight implementations, highlighting similarities and differences among them. Furthermore, we examine multiple parameter settings, optimization strategies, and implementation-specific features to demonstrate how parameter configuration can affect performance and how systematic evaluation can reveal non-obvious trade-offs. The results show significant performance differences, up to two orders of magnitude in some cases, not only between different implementations when aligning parameters, but also within the same implementation when comparing different parameter configurations. Hence, our results demonstrate the significant value and insight that can be gained from conducting rigorous performance evaluations. Using our results and framework as a starting point, more rigorous benchmarking will ultimately help users and developers make informed decisions and support future development efforts to build better, more efficient software.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a performance-oriented benchmarking framework for comparing DMRG (density matrix renormalization group) software implementations, applies it to eight implementations, and reveals performance differences up to two orders of magnitude both across implementations and parameter configurations, demonstrating the value of systematic performance evaluation.
AI.motivation: With over 50 DMRG software implementations available, systematic performance evaluation is needed to compare their strengths and limitations. However, existing evaluations are scarce, lack a consistent standard, are often too incomplete for meaningful comparisons, or focus on objectives other than direct performance comparison.
AI.method: The authors develop a performance-oriented benchmarking framework and apply it to quantify the performance of eight DMRG implementations. They examine multiple parameter settings, optimization strategies, and implementation-specific features to assess how configuration affects performance and to reveal non-obvious trade-offs.
AI.result: Significant performance differences were found, up to two orders of magnitude in some cases, both between different implementations (when parameters are aligned) and within the same implementation (across different parameter configurations). The framework successfully highlights similarities and differences among the eight implementations.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous performance evaluations provide significant value and insight for DMRG implementations. The framework serves as a starting point for more rigorous benchmarking, ultimately helping users and developers make informed decisions and supporting future development of more efficient software.

title: Semilinear Elliptic Systems with Nonlocal Homogeneous Critical Nonlinearities
summary: This paper concerns a variational system of nonlinear elliptic equations that generalizes the classical Brezis-Nirenberg problem. In addition to considering vector-valued unknown functions in place of scalar-valued unknown functions, the problem under consideration generalizes the Brezis-Nirenberg problem in two directions. First, the nonlinearity is the sum of two homogeneous functions of suitable homogeneity degrees. Second, the Sobolev-critical term in the nonlinearity is nonlocal. We establish conditions under which a nontrivial solution to the system under consideration is guaranteed to exist and conditions under which the system under consideration admits only the trivial solution.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a variational system of nonlinear elliptic equations that generalizes the classical Brezis-Nirenberg problem in two ways: (1) the nonlinearity is a sum of two homogeneous functions of suitable degrees, and (2) the Sobolev-critical term is nonlocal. The authors establish conditions for both the existence of nontrivial solutions and conditions under which only the trivial solution exists.
AI.motivation: To extend the classical Brezis-Nirenberg problem by generalizing it from scalar to vector-valued unknown functions, incorporating a sum of homogeneous nonlinearities, and introducing a nonlocal Sobolev-critical term—broadening the applicability of this well-known problem in nonlinear analysis.
AI.method: The paper considers a variational system of nonlinear elliptic equations with vector-valued unknown functions. The nonlinearity is composed of two homogeneous functions with suitable homogeneity degrees, and the Sobolev-critical term is nonlocal. The analysis establishes existence and non-existence conditions for solutions to this system.
AI.result: Conditions are derived that guarantee the existence of a nontrivial solution to the system, as well as conditions under which the system admits only the trivial solution.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete characterization of existence and non-existence regimes for the generalized Brezis-Nirenberg variational system with nonlocal critical nonlinearities and multiple homogeneous terms.

title: Dynamical Low-Rank Smoothing
summary: Computational costs often make smoothing procedures prohibitive for high-dimensional data assimilation problems. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) methodology for smoothing concerning frameworks based on stochastic differential equations. We extend the previously developed joint mean-and-covariance optimization (JMCO) filtering setting to derive a reduced-order smoother via the Rauch--Tung--Striebel recursion and establish the corresponding Kalman--Bucy smoothing for affine drift dynamics. The resulting algorithms retain the adaptive nature of DLRA while significantly reducing the computational time and storage of the whole smoothing procedure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) methodology for smoothing in high-dimensional data assimilation problems based on stochastic differential equations, extending the joint mean-and-covariance optimization (JMCO) filtering framework to derive a reduced-order smoother via Rauch-Tung-Striebel recursion and Kalman-Bucy smoothing for affine drift dynamics.
AI.motivation: Computational costs make smoothing procedures prohibitive for high-dimensional data assimilation problems, motivating the need for a more efficient approach.
AI.method: Extends the JMCO filtering setting to derive a reduced-order smoother via the Rauch-Tung-Striebel recursion and establishes Kalman-Bucy smoothing for affine drift dynamics using DLRA.
AI.result: The algorithms retain the adaptive nature of DLRA while significantly reducing computational time and storage of the entire smoothing procedure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DLRA-based smoothing framework offers a computationally efficient solution for high-dimensional data assimilation problems without sacrificing adaptivity.

title: Coaxial Gyromagnetic Nonlinear Transmission Line with a Slow-Wave Structure: 2D/3D FDTD Modeling
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Plasma Science (Manuscript ID: TPS18901). Materials of this paper were presented as a poster report "2D/3D FDTD Modeling of Coaxial Waveguide with Magnetized Nonlinear Ferrite and Slow-Wave Structure" at the XXXII International Workshop on Optical Wave & Waveguide Theory and Numerical Modelling, 8-10 April 2026, Lausanne, Switzerland (https://owtnm26.epfl.ch/)
summary: A coaxial gyromagnetic nonlinear transmission line (GNLTL) enables pulse-front compression and oscillation packet generation in the 0.3-10 GHz range. Numerical modeling of such systems typically employs a 2D axially symmetric FDTD scheme coupled with the parallel solution of full non-linearized Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations. Previous studies have shown that using an insulating dielectric with a permittivity $ε$>60 enables the generation of long-lasting oscillations via a Cherenkov-like effect. However, practical implementation is limited due to the severe high-frequency losses inherent in materials with such extreme permittivity, like water. To overcome this limitation and enhance performance, we propose a novel design utilizing a spiral central conductor to mimic a high-permittivity environment, with the ferrite placed inside the spiral. Due to the loss of axial symmetry, the FDTD model was extended to 3D coordinates. Simulations confirm that the spiral conductor configuration generates a prolonged oscillation packet similar to that of a high-permittivity dielectric waveguide, but with significantly reduced losses and improved energy transfer efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel coaxial gyromagnetic nonlinear transmission line (GNLTL) design using a spiral central conductor with ferrite placed inside to mimic high-permittivity environments, enabling pulse-front compression and oscillation packet generation (0.3-10 GHz) with reduced losses compared to traditional high-permittivity dielectric approaches.
AI.motivation: Previous GNLTL designs relied on high-permittivity dielectrics (ε>60) to generate long-lasting oscillations via a Cherenkov-like effect, but practical implementation is hampered by severe high-frequency losses in such materials (e.g., water). A new approach is needed to achieve similar performance with significantly lower losses.
AI.method: A spiral central conductor is used to emulate a high-permittivity environment, with the ferrite placed inside the spiral. Since this design breaks axial symmetry, the numerical model was extended from a 2D axially symmetric FDTD scheme (coupled with full non-linearized Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations) to a 3D FDTD model.
AI.result: Simulations confirm that the spiral conductor configuration generates a prolonged oscillation packet similar to that produced by a high-permittivity dielectric waveguide, but with significantly reduced losses and improved energy transfer efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The spiral conductor design offers a practical alternative to high-permittivity dielectrics for GNLTL applications, achieving comparable oscillation generation performance while overcoming the loss limitations of extreme-permittivity materials.

title: Fast and Accurate Foundation Models for Equivariant Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a transformative tool for computational materials science and chemistry, with universal potentials trained on large and diverse datasets now routinely deployed as 'foundation models' for downstream fine-tuning in targeted chemical spaces. Many scientific applications of the resulting models, such as molecular dynamics (MD), require high inference and training speeds as well as accuracy. In this work, we examine the limits of equivariant MLIPs, which directly encode physical symmetries in model architectures, to achieve these competing targets -- particularly in the regime of extremely large datasets where data efficiency is less critical. We show how this trade-off can be addressed, and present a family of foundation potentials in the NequIP and Allegro equivariant MLIP architectures which achieve leading inference speeds and strong scalability as well as excellent accuracies across a range of community benchmarks -- spanning materials discovery, thermal conductivity prediction, and near-equilibrium mechanical and thermodynamic properties. Accelerations implemented within the NequIP infrastructure now permit training of high-accuracy foundation potentials on ultra-large datasets with dramatically reduced computational cost. Alongside, we show that efforts to improve model accuracy for materials discovery should focus on dataset diversity and improved, consistent descriptions of transition metal compound energy surfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the limits and trade-offs of equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for large-scale applications, presenting a family of foundation potentials built on NequIP and Allegro architectures that achieve leading inference speeds, strong scalability, and excellent accuracy across multiple materials science benchmarks. The work includes infrastructure optimizations enabling training on ultra-large datasets at dramatically reduced cost, and highlights that further accuracy gains for materials discovery should prioritize dataset diversity and improved transition metal compound energy surface descriptions.
AI.motivation: Universal MLIPs are increasingly used as foundation models for downstream fine-tuning, but many scientific applications (e.g., molecular dynamics) require simultaneously high inference/training speeds and accuracy. The authors aim to examine whether equivariant MLIPs, which encode physical symmetries architecturally, can achieve these competing targets—especially in the ultra-large dataset regime where data efficiency matters less.
AI.method: The authors analyze the trade-offs of equivariant MLIP architectures and present optimized foundation potentials based on NequIP and Allegro. They implement computational accelerations within the NequIP infrastructure to enable training on ultra-large datasets, and benchmark the resulting models across community datasets spanning materials discovery, thermal conductivity prediction, and near-equilibrium mechanical and thermodynamic properties.
AI.result: The proposed family of equivariant foundation potentials achieves leading inference speeds, strong scalability, and excellent accuracy across diverse benchmarks. Training accelerations substantially reduce computational cost for ultra-large dataset training. Benchmark analyses further reveal that improving materials discovery accuracy should focus on dataset diversity and consistent descriptions of transition metal compound energy surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Equivariant MLIPs can effectively balance speed, scalability, and accuracy even in the large-data regime when properly optimized. The key bottleneck for further accuracy improvement in materials discovery is not solely model architecture but dataset diversity and the quality of energy surface descriptions for transition metal compounds.

title: Remarks on some quasi-linear fourth order parabolic equations arising in mathematical physics
summary: This note proves existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to a broad class of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations in the class of Wiener spaces. It improves upon previous results in the literature, devoted to some special cases falling within the general framework developed here, in which uniqueness held true in a smaller class than the space where existence was proven. Gain of analyticity, as well as generalisations to higher-order equations and to propagation of higher regularities, are also discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper proves existence and uniqueness of strong solutions for a broad class of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations on Wiener spaces, improving on prior special-case results by establishing uniqueness in the same class where existence is proven. It also discusses gain of analyticity, generalizations to higher-order equations, and propagation of higher regularities.
AI.motivation: Previous literature only addressed special cases of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations on Wiener spaces, and in those cases uniqueness was proven only in a smaller class than the space where existence held. The authors aim to develop a general framework that overcomes this gap by proving both existence and uniqueness in the same space.
AI.method: The paper develops a general framework for fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations on Wiener spaces, proving existence and uniqueness of strong solutions. It also addresses gain of analyticity, extensions to higher-order equations, and propagation of higher regularities.
AI.result: The paper proves existence and uniqueness of strong solutions for a broad class of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations on Wiener spaces, improving prior results by establishing uniqueness in the full space where existence is shown, rather than a restricted subspace.
AI.conclusion: The general framework unifies and improves previous special-case results, and the methods extend to higher-order equations, analyticity gain, and propagation of higher regularities.

title: Residual-Driven Lifting Identification for Nonlinear-Manifold Reduced-Order Models of Parametrized Linear PDEs
summary: We introduce a residual-driven procedure for training nonlinear-manifold reduced-order models for parametrized linear partial differential equations that, given prescribed latent and lifting spaces, identifies the nonlinear lifting without high-fidelity solution snapshots. The approximation is represented by a low-dimensional latent coordinate together with a nonlinear lifting into a richer reduced space. Rather than fitting the lifting to snapshot data, we determine it by minimizing a computable residual-based upper bound for the state error. For affinely parametrized operators, the resulting training objective admits an efficient offline--online decomposition, and the lifting update reduces to a sequence of low-dimensional weighted least-squares problems. Numerical evaluations on an advection--diffusion problem and a plane-strain elasticity benchmark show that the proposed approach substantially improves accuracy over linear subspaces. The resulting nonlinear models achieve accuracy comparable to snapshot-driven nonlinear-manifold training while avoiding high-fidelity snapshots in the lifting-identification stage.

AI.tldr: A residual-driven training procedure for nonlinear-manifold reduced-order models that identifies nonlinear liftings without requiring high-fidelity solution snapshots, using a residual-based upper bound on state error as the training objective.
AI.motivation: Traditional nonlinear-manifold reduced-order models rely on high-fidelity solution snapshots to train the nonlinear lifting, which is costly and data-intensive. This work aims to eliminate that dependency by deriving the lifting from residual information instead.
AI.method: Given prescribed latent and lifting spaces, the nonlinear lifting is identified by minimizing a computable residual-based upper bound for the state error, rather than fitting to snapshots. For affinely parametrized operators, the training objective admits an efficient offline-online decomposition, and the lifting update reduces to a sequence of low-dimensional weighted least-squares problems.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on advection-diffusion and plane-strain elasticity problems show the proposed approach substantially improves accuracy over linear subspaces and achieves accuracy comparable to snapshot-driven nonlinear-manifold training, while avoiding high-fidelity snapshots in the lifting-identification stage.
AI.conclusion: Residual-based training can replace snapshot-based training for nonlinear-manifold ROMs, offering comparable accuracy at lower data cost and providing a practical alternative to linear subspace models.

title: The Second Quadratic Invariant of Astrophysical Gyrokinetics
summary: We show that gyrokinetics in a spatially uniform equilibrium (or `astrophysical gyrokinetics') possesses a previously unknown quadratic invariant, which we call the gyrokinetic helicity. We derive the limiting forms of the gyrokinetic helicity in five subsidiary expansions of astrophysical gyrokinetics: the isothermal electron fluid (ITEF) approximation, kinetic reduced magnetohydrodynamics (KRMHD), electron reduced magnetohydrodynamics (ERMHD), finite-Larmor-radius magnetohydrodynamics (FLR-MHD), and the kinetic reduced electron heating model~(KREHM). We subdivide the real part of the gyrokinetic helicity into `magnetofluid' and `phase-space' components, which are separately conserved in KRMHD, ERMHD, and FLR-MHD (in which there is no phase-space helicity). The magnetofluid helicity is equivalent to the Alfvénic part of the cross helicity in KRMHD, the magnetic helicity in~ERMHD, and the generalized helicity in FLR-MHD and~KREHM. We derive an analytic expression for the rate at which magnetofluid helicity is converted into phase-space helicity at length scales comparable to the proton gyroradius in the ITEF approximation. We also explain how this conversion circumvents the helicity barrier and enhances turbulent heating in coronal holes and the near-Sun solar wind.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers a new quadratic invariant in astrophysical gyrokinetics called the gyrokinetic helicity, derives its limiting forms across five subsidiary approximations (ITEF, KRMHD, ERMHD, FLR-MHD, KREHM), decomposes it into magnetofluid and phase-space components, and shows how their conversion at proton gyroradius scales bypasses the helicity barrier to enhance turbulent heating in coronal holes and the near-Sun solar wind.
AI.motivation: To identify a previously unknown conserved quantity in gyrokinetics that can unify understanding of helicity conservation across multiple plasma approximations and explain the helicity barrier and turbulent heating mechanisms in astrophysical plasmas.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of the gyrokinetic helicity invariant from gyrokinetics in a spatially uniform equilibrium, followed by its limiting-form derivation in five subsidiary expansions (ITEF, KRMHD, ERMHD, FLR-MHD, KREHM). The invariant is decomposed into magnetofluid and phase-space components, and an analytic expression is derived for the magnetofluid-to-phase-space helicity conversion rate at proton gyroradius scales in the ITEF approximation.
AI.result: The gyrokinetic helicity is identified as a new quadratic invariant. Its magnetofluid component maps to the Alfvénic cross helicity in KRMHD, magnetic helicity in ERMHD, and generalized helicity in FLR-MHD and KREHM. The magnetofluid and phase-space components are separately conserved in KRMHD, ERMHD, and FLR-MHD. An analytic conversion rate between components is derived in ITEF, explaining how this conversion circumvents the helicity barrier and enhances turbulent heating.
AI.conclusion: The gyrokinetic helicity provides a unifying framework for helicity conservation across plasma models and reveals a mechanism by which helicity transfer between magnetofluid and phase-space channels at proton gyroradius scales enables turbulent energy to dissipate, overcoming the helicity barrier in coronal holes and the near-Sun solar wind.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for 2D Plane Wave Scattering in Arbitrary Dielectric Structures
summary: In this paper, we introduce a meshless physics-informed neural network based computational framework for solving two-dimensional electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media. The framework embeds frequency-domain Maxwell equations and radiation boundary conditions directly into the neural network loss function, enabling accurate prediction of scattered fields for both transverse magnetic (TM) and transverse electric (TE) polarizations across various dielectric configurations. Application of the method to single-cylinder, concentric multilayer cylindrical shells, three arbitrarily arranged cylinders, and composite irregular structures demonstrates that for the TM polarization, all relative $L^{2}$ errors mostly remain at particularly low levels of $\le0.1$. For the TE polarization, sharp variations of the dielectric properties of scatterers lead to singularities in the governing equations, which result in decreased accuracy of the method. This challenge is overcome by introducing at dielectric boundaries a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function. This procedure significantly improves the accuracy of the method, with the corresponding results closely matching the predictions of the finite-difference time-domain method. This framework exhibits stable convergence behavior across all of the investigated configurations, thus confirming its robustness and scalability to complex electromagnetic scattering problems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a meshless physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for solving 2D electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media. The method embeds frequency-domain Maxwell's equations and radiation boundary conditions into the neural network loss function. It handles both TM and TE polarizations across various dielectric configurations including cylinders, multilayer shells, and irregular structures. TM polarization achieves low relative L2 errors (≤0.1), while TE polarization challenges from dielectric singularities are resolved using a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function at boundaries, with results matching FDTD predictions.
AI.motivation: To develop a meshless computational framework for solving 2D electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media without traditional meshing, addressing both TM and TE polarizations while handling numerical challenges posed by sharp dielectric property variations in TE cases.
AI.method: A physics-informed neural network framework that embeds frequency-domain Maxwell equations and radiation boundary conditions directly into the loss function. For TE polarization, a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function is introduced at dielectric boundaries to eliminate singularities in the governing equations caused by sharp dielectric property variations.
AI.result: For TM polarization, all relative L2 errors remain mostly at extremely low levels (≤0.1) across all tested configurations (single cylinder, concentric multilayer shells, three cylinders, composite irregular structures). For TE polarization, initial accuracy issues from dielectric singularities were overcome with the smoothing function, yielding results that closely match FDTD predictions. The framework exhibits stable convergence across all configurations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PINN-based framework is robust and scalable for complex electromagnetic scattering problems, demonstrating accuracy for TM polarization and effective handling of TE polarization challenges through boundary smoothing, with stable convergence behavior confirmed across all investigated configurations.

title: Rigorous justification of the hydrostatic-incompressible approximation for weakly stratified isothermal flow
summary: We consider the limit of small Mach number and small vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio for the isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes system. In addition, we consider the scale in which the stratification is weak. Owing to the anisotropic nature of the problem, the dynamics exhibit a three-wave separation phenomenon, consistent of a slow wave, a fast horizontal acoustic wave, and an even faster vertical acoustic wave. These three waves, unfortunately, are not mutually orthogonal, and the corresponding projections are parametrized by the small parameter, which significantly complicates the nonlinear analysis. Without any restriction on the size of the initial waves, we establish the uniform existence and uniqueness of solutions to the compressible Navier-Stokes system for any fixed small parameter, by carefully analyzing the evolutions of both the energy and the acoustic waves. Moreover, we prove that, as the small parameter tends to zero, the solutions converge to that of the incompressible primitive equations governing atmospheric and oceanic flows.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the low Mach number and low aspect ratio limits of the isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes system with weak stratification, revealing a three-wave separation phenomenon (slow, fast horizontal acoustic, and faster vertical acoustic waves). The authors establish uniform existence and uniqueness of solutions for any fixed small parameter without restrictions on initial wave size, and prove convergence to the incompressible primitive equations as the small parameter approaches zero.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to rigorously justify the derivation of the incompressible primitive equations (governing atmospheric and oceanic flows) from the compressible Navier-Stokes system under simultaneous low Mach number and low aspect ratio limits. The key challenge is that the three wave modes arising from the anisotropic problem are not mutually orthogonal, and their projections depend on the small parameter, which complicates the nonlinear analysis.
AI.method: The authors analyze the joint limit of small Mach number, small aspect ratio, and weak stratification in the isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes system. They identify a three-wave separation structure (slow, fast horizontal acoustic, and faster vertical acoustic waves) and carefully track the evolutions of both energy and acoustic waves to handle the non-orthogonality of the wave modes. The analysis proceeds without any restriction on the size of the initial waves.
AI.result: The authors establish uniform existence and uniqueness of solutions for any fixed small parameter, and prove convergence of solutions to those of the incompressible primitive equations as the small parameter tends to zero.
AI.conclusion: The compressible Navier-Stokes system with small Mach number, small aspect ratio, and weak stratification converges to the incompressible primitive equations, providing a rigorous theoretical justification for these atmospheric/oceanic models.

title: Scalable Graph Coreset Selection via Greedy Sampling
summary: Sampling representative nodes from large graphs is fundamental to graph signal processing and network analysis, yet existing methods require access to the full graph Laplacian, making them impractical at scale. We propose a simple and effective column-selective graph sampling algorithm based on a minimum inner product greedy selection rule. At each iteration, the algorithm accesses only a small random subset of Laplacian columns, requiring no eigendecomposition or global graph traversal, making it well-suited for large-scale graphs where the full Laplacian cannot be stored in memory. We analyze the algorithm under the stochastic block model and show that, when the degree distribution is balanced across nodes, the algorithm achieves sampling proportional to cluster size, and that the resulting mean estimate is controlled for band-limited graph signals in the Paley-Wiener space, with the error decaying as inter-cluster connectivity weakens. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A scalable column-selective graph sampling algorithm using a minimum inner product greedy rule that accesses only random subsets of Laplacian columns per iteration, avoiding eigendecomposition and full graph traversal. The algorithm is theoretically analyzed under the stochastic block model, and validated on synthetic and real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing graph sampling methods require access to the full graph Laplacian (often via eigendecomposition), which is impractical for large-scale graphs that cannot be stored in memory. There is a need for a sampling method that works at scale without global graph access.
AI.method: A minimum inner product greedy selection rule that iteratively samples columns of the Laplacian. At each iteration, only a small random subset of columns is accessed, requiring no eigendecomposition or global graph traversal.
AI.result: Under the stochastic block model with balanced degree distribution, the algorithm achieves sampling proportional to cluster size. The mean estimate error is bounded for band-limited graph signals in the Paley-Wiener space, decaying as inter-cluster connectivity weakens. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs confirm effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed greedy column-selective algorithm provides an efficient, scalable solution for graph sampling that avoids the computational bottlenecks of existing methods while offering theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.

title: Effect of confinement anisotropy on particle transport and structural relaxation of finite dust clusters in complex plasma
summary: A finite dusty plasma cluster of charged microparticles confined in an anisotropic potential well is investigated experimentally and through Langevin dynamics simulations. As the confinement anisotropy is increased, the cluster undergoes a structural transition from near isotropic concentric shells to a linear chain configuration. The spatiotemporal modes of the cluster are analyzed by using Singular Value Decomposition. At weaker confinement anisotropies, two modes are dominant. Mode 1, corresponding to a breathing-type oscillation of the cluster, and mode 2, representing an azimuthal rotational motion of the cluster, together carry around 99$\%$ of the signal energy. With increasing anisotropy, the dominance of mode 2 decreases and that of mode 1 increases. This mode restructuring is accompanied by an increasingly non-Gaussian particle displacement statistics as evidenced by positive values of the Non-Gaussian Parameter maintained over an extended time duration. Simultaneously, the increasing dominance of mode 1 and suppression of mode 2 is accompanied by a significant slowing down of structural relaxation, with the cluster eventually exhibiting signatures of structural arrest. At weaker anisotropy, the experimentally measured dynamical quantities are very sensitive to the initial conditions which account for the discrepancy between the experiment and initial condition averaged simulation results for these observables. This study offers insight into the mechanisms underlying anomalous transport and structural relaxation in anisotropically confined many-body systems.

AI.tldr: A study of finite dusty plasma clusters in anisotropic potential wells, showing that increasing confinement anisotropy drives a structural transition from concentric shells to linear chains, accompanied by mode restructuring (from rotational to breathing dominance), non-Gaussian dynamics, and structural arrest.
AI.motivation: To understand how confinement anisotropy affects structural transitions, spatiotemporal modes, transport properties, and structural relaxation in finite many-body systems, providing insight into anomalous transport mechanisms in anisotropically confined systems.
AI.method: Experiments with charged microparticles in a dusty plasma confined in an anisotropic potential well, complemented by Langevin dynamics simulations. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is used to analyze spatiotemporal modes, and Non-Gaussian Parameter is used to characterize particle displacement statistics.
AI.result: At weak anisotropy, two dominant modes (breathing oscillation and azimuthal rotation) carry ~99% of signal energy. Increasing anisotropy shifts dominance from mode 2 (rotation) to mode 1 (breathing), accompanied by positive non-Gaussian parameter over extended durations, slowing structural relaxation, and eventual structural arrest. Experimental quantities are sensitive to initial conditions at weak anisotropy, explaining discrepancies with simulation averages.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals how anisotropy-driven mode restructuring couples to anomalous transport and structural arrest in confined many-body systems, offering mechanistic insight into these phenomena.

title: A sub-grid-scale model for polydisperse bubbly flows with heat and mass transfer
summary: Ensemble-averaged models of polydisperse bubbly flows require statistics of the evolving bubble population. Prior quadrature-based moment formulations close bubble pressure with a polytropic relation that omits heat and mass transfer at the bubble wall. We formulate constant-transfer equations for bubble pressure and vapor mass within a conditional hyperbolic quadrature method. Second-order conditional inversion produces four joint radius--radial-velocity nodes per equilibrium-radius bin. Bubble pressure and vapor mass are advanced at each node. The node values close the ensemble-averaged flow equations without adding mixed pressure or vapor-mass moments to the transported moment set. The model is implemented in MFC. Monte Carlo calculations verify the evolution of quadrature nodes and the mean bubble variables for a harmonically forced population. Bubble-screen calculations quantify closure error as the equilibrium radius is discretized and the initial distributions vary. The constant-transfer calculation does not exhibit the high-frequency pressure oscillations observed with the polytropic closure under the conditions considered. 3D bubble-screen calculations give a 1.5% relative root-mean-square error between the Euler--Euler center pressure and the mean of 40 volume-averaged Euler--Lagrange realizations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a conditional hyperbolic quadrature method for polydisperse bubbly flows that advances bubble pressure and vapor mass at each quadrature node using constant-transfer equations, avoiding the high-frequency oscillations seen with polytropic closures. The model is validated against Monte Carlo and Euler-Lagrange simulations, achieving 1.5% RMS error in 3D bubble-screen tests.
AI.motivation: Ensemble-averaged polydisperse bubbly flow models need statistics of the evolving bubble population. Prior quadrature-based moment methods close bubble pressure with a polytropic relation that omits heat and mass transfer at the bubble wall, which is a significant physical limitation.
AI.method: Formulates constant-transfer equations for bubble pressure and vapor mass within a conditional hyperbolic quadrature method. Uses second-order conditional inversion to produce four joint radius-radial-velocity nodes per equilibrium-radius bin, advancing bubble pressure and vapor mass at each node to close ensemble-averaged flow equations without adding extra moments. Implemented in the MFC code.
AI.result: Monte Carlo calculations verify quadrature node evolution and mean bubble variables for harmonically forced populations. Bubble-screen calculations quantify closure error as a function of equilibrium radius discretization and initial distribution. The constant-transfer closure avoids high-frequency pressure oscillations seen with polytropic closure. 3D calculations show 1.5% relative RMS error between Euler-Euler and averaged Euler-Lagrange realizations.
AI.conclusion: The constant-transfer conditional hyperbolic quadrature method provides accurate and physically improved closure for polydisperse bubbly flows, eliminating spurious oscillations and achieving good agreement with high-fidelity Euler-Lagrange simulations.

title: On the upper bound for the vorticity growth of bi-rotational Euler flows without swirl
summary: For $d\geq 4$, we consider incompressible Euler flows in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with bi-rotational symmetry and without swirl. Our first result gives the local wellposedness of the Yudovich-type solution. The second result provides global wellposedness up to $d\leq 6$. In particular, it shows that the rate of growth of the vorticity maximum coincides with the rate from axisymmetric flows without swirl, which was obtained in the paper by the second author and Jeong (Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 249(3):32, 2025) and Shao--Wei--Zhang (Acta Math. Sin. (Engl. Ser.), 42(3):663-679, 2026).

AI.tldr: This paper studies incompressible Euler flows in R^d (d≥4) with bi-rotational symmetry and without swirl, proving local wellposedness of Yudovich-type solutions and global wellposedness up to d≤6, with vorticity growth rates matching axisymmetric flows without swirl.
AI.motivation: To extend wellposedness results for Euler equations with symmetry beyond the axisymmetric case, specifically analyzing bi-rotational symmetry in higher dimensions (d≥4) and understanding vorticity growth behavior in this setting.
AI.method: The paper develops a Yudovich-type solution framework for bi-rotational symmetric Euler flows without swirl, presumably using energy estimates and special structure exploiting the bi-rotational symmetry to control vorticity growth.
AI.result: Local wellposedness of Yudovich-type solutions is established for all d≥4, and global wellposedness is achieved for d≤6. The vorticity maximum growth rate matches that of axisymmetric flows without swirl.
AI.conclusion: The bi-rotational symmetry structure permits wellposedness results analogous to the axisymmetric case, with the dimension threshold d≤6 for global wellposedness, and vorticity growth rates consistent with previously known axisymmetric results.

title: A novel sampling method for reconstruction of a moving point acoustic source in $\mathbb{R}^3$
summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel sampling method to recovering the trajectory of a moving point source in R^3, where both the spatial location and emission moment of the moving point source are unknown. Combining algebraic theory with geometric knowledge, we prove the uniqueness of the source location by using measured data from five observation points. Our sampling method constructs an indicator function based on the property that the residual of the time difference of arrival constraint formula vanishes at the true source location. It achieves the reconstruction of the spatial positions and emission moments of a moving point source only using data from five observation points and their corresponding arrival times. The algorithm not only reduces the required number of observation points, but also improves computational efficiency, stability, and noise resistance. Numerical experiments verify the effectiveness of the method.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel sampling method for reconstructing the trajectory of a moving point source in R^3 with unknown spatial locations and emission moments, using only five observation points. The method combines algebraic theory with geometric knowledge to prove uniqueness of source location and constructs an indicator function based on the vanishing residual of a time difference of arrival constraint at the true source location, achieving improvements in computational efficiency, stability, and noise resistance.
AI.motivation: To recover the trajectory of a moving point source in 3D space when both the spatial location and emission time are unknown, while reducing the number of required observation points and improving computational efficiency and robustness.
AI.method: A sampling method that combines algebraic theory with geometric knowledge to prove uniqueness of source location using five observation points. An indicator function is constructed based on the property that the residual of the time difference of arrival constraint formula vanishes at the true source location, enabling reconstruction of both spatial positions and emission moments.
AI.result: The method requires only five observation points, reduces the required number of observation points compared to prior approaches, and improves computational efficiency, stability, and noise resistance. Numerical experiments verify its effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed sampling method successfully reconstructs moving point source trajectories in R^3 with fewer observation points while maintaining robustness, as confirmed by numerical experiments.

title: Electromagnetically Driven Thermal Dissipation Scaling in Plasma Centrifuges for Mass Separation
summary: Electromagnetically driven centrifuges (EMDCs) rotate fluids using the Lorentz force, but their separative performance is limited by thermal dissipation that is coupled to electromagnetic forcing. This follows because local centrifugal strength is proportional to λ=mV_θ^2/2k_B T, which compares directed kinetic energy that drives species separation to thermal energy that smooths concentration gradients and counteracts separation. In this work, we develop a reduced two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic model to determine how radial geometry, current density, and magnetic field strength control the coupled evolution of rotation and heating that dictates λ. The model is benchmarked against Ar and Ar/Kr experiments spanning current density up to 15 kA/m^2, magnetic field up to 0.57 T, feed pressures of 0.5-3 Torr, and annulus sizes of 1-5 cm. The results show that volumetric Lorentz forcing sustains higher λ and therefore greater local compositional shifts throughout a larger radial portion of the fluid volume than wall-bounded shear centrifuges, despite lower peak λ. Simulations of a 40Ar/36Ar isotopic mixture demonstrate that, when electromagnetic force and geometry are jointly optimized, EMDCs can exceed the separative performance of shear-driven centrifuges operating near material speed limits, for lower area-averaged values of λ. These results challenge assertions that viscous dissipation constrains weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1, and indicate that enhanced radial mass separation can be achieved by increasing the radial distribution of λ rather than maximizing its peak or area-averaged value.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a reduced two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic model for electromagnetically driven centrifuges (EMDCs), showing that volumetric Lorentz forcing distributes centrifugal strength (λ) more broadly across the fluid volume than wall-bounded shear centrifuges, enabling EMDCs to exceed the separative performance of shear-driven centrifuges when jointly optimizing electromagnetic force and geometry.
AI.motivation: EMDCs rotate fluids via the Lorentz force, but their separation performance is limited by thermal dissipation coupled to electromagnetic forcing. The key parameter λ= mV_θ²/2k_BT compares directed kinetic energy (driving separation) to thermal energy (smoothing gradients), and it is unclear how geometry, current, and magnetic field control the coupled rotation-heating evolution. Prior work also asserted that viscous dissipation constrains weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1, which this paper challenges.
AI.method: The authors develop a reduced two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model that captures the coupled evolution of rotation and heating. The model is benchmarked against Ar and Ar/Kr experiments across a wide parameter space: current densities up to 15 kA/m², magnetic fields up to 0.57 T, feed pressures of 0.5–3 Torr, and annulus sizes of 1–5 cm. Simulations are then performed for 40Ar/36Ar isotopic mixtures.
AI.result: Volumetric Lorentz forcing sustains higher λ and greater local compositional shifts across a larger radial portion of the fluid than wall-bounded shear centrifuges, despite lower peak λ. For 40Ar/36Ar mixtures, jointly optimized EMDCs can exceed the separative performance of shear-driven centrifuges operating near material speed limits, even at lower area-averaged λ values.
AI.conclusion: The results challenge the assertion that viscous dissipation limits weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1. Enhanced radial mass separation is achieved by increasing the radial distribution of λ rather than maximizing its peak or area-averaged value, offering a new design strategy for EMDC optimization.

title: Design principles for energy dissipation in viscoelastic network metamaterials
summary: Mechanical energy dissipation in networked materials is relevant for applications from vibration isolation to impact protection, yet identifying optimal dissipative architectures in large disordered truss networks is computationally prohibitive with conventional finite element methods. We develop an efficient graph Laplacian-based spectral framework for viscoelastic truss networks, in which the full continuum dynamics of each rod are retained exactly and the problem size scales with the number of joints rather than element-level discretization points. Using this framework, we investigate how redistributing cross-sectional areas within a network (without changing material composition) controls energy dissipation. We find that random redistribution typically reduces dissipation relative to a uniform baseline, while gradient-based optimization yields nontrivial architectures whose form is governed by the intrinsic attenuation length of the base material. Focusing on driving frequencies near a global resonant mode of the network, we show that the optimal mass distribution decays from the source (driven joint) with the attenuation length scale, and at small attenuation lengths the optimal architecture is independent of the boundary conditions. These results motivate future studies of dissipation length scale based design principles on more complex disordered architectures and provide an efficient computational framework for exploring such structures at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an efficient graph Laplacian-based spectral framework for analyzing viscoelastic truss networks, allowing full continuum dynamics to be retained while scaling with the number of joints rather than discretization points. Using this framework, the authors investigate how redistributing cross-sectional areas controls energy dissipation, finding that random redistribution typically reduces dissipation, while gradient-based optimization yields optimal architectures governed by the material's intrinsic attenuation length, with the optimal mass distribution decaying exponentially from the driven joint.
AI.motivation: Mechanical energy dissipation in networked materials is critical for vibration isolation and impact protection, but identifying optimal dissipative architectures in large disordered truss networks is computationally prohibitive using conventional finite element methods.
AI.method: The authors develop a graph Laplacian-based spectral framework for viscoelastic truss networks that exactly retains the full continuum dynamics of each rod while scaling problem size with the number of joints rather than element-level discretization. They use this to study how redistributing cross-sectional areas affects energy dissipation, comparing random redistribution against gradient-based optimization approaches.
AI.result: Random redistribution typically reduces dissipation relative to a uniform baseline, while gradient-based optimization produces nontrivial architectures governed by the intrinsic attenuation length of the base material. Near a global resonant mode, the optimal mass distribution decays from the driven joint at the attenuation length scale, and at small attenuation lengths the optimal architecture becomes independent of boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate future studies of dissipation length scale-based design principles for more complex disordered architectures and provide an efficient computational framework for exploring such structures at scale.

title: Incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier limit from a nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation
summary: We derive the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier limit from a nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation with Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics. The model has a self-consistent collision structure, with the local density acting as the collision frequency and the bulk velocity and temperature determined by nonlinear quantum-weighted moments of the distribution. We work near a global quantum equilibrium under the diffusive scaling and keep the quantum parameter fixed. Uniform estimates with respect to the Knudsen number yield strong microscopic relaxation and identify the limiting infinitesimal quantum equilibrium. Using the local conservation laws, we prove the incompressibility condition, the Boussinesq relation, and strong compactness of the divergence-free velocity component and a quantum-adapted thermal mode, while the acoustic modes vanish locally by a dispersive estimate. The limiting viscous stress tensor and heat flux are identified by solving auxiliary equations for the linearized quantum Fokker-Planck operator and by expanding the local quantum equilibrium manifold. The resulting incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier system retains the effect of quantum statistics through its normalization constants and transport coefficients.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier limit from a nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation with Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics, proving uniform estimates, strong compactness, and identifying transport coefficients under diffusive scaling with fixed quantum parameter.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous hydrodynamic limit connecting quantum kinetic models with classical fluid dynamics, showing how quantum statistics (Bose-Einstein/Fermi-Dirac) survive in the macroscopic Navier-Stokes-Fourier system through normalization constants and transport coefficients.
AI.method: The authors work near a global quantum equilibrium under diffusive scaling with fixed quantum parameter. They employ uniform estimates with respect to the Knudsen number, local conservation laws for the incompressibility condition and Boussinesq relation, a dispersive estimate to show acoustic modes vanish locally, solve auxiliary equations for the linearized quantum Fokker-Planck operator, and expand the local quantum equilibrium manifold to identify viscous stress tensor and heat flux.
AI.result: The limiting system is the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations, which retain quantum statistical effects through normalization constants and transport coefficients. Strong microscopic relaxation to an infinitesimal quantum equilibrium is established, along with strong compactness of the divergence-free velocity component and a quantum-adapted thermal mode.
AI.conclusion: The incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier limit is rigorously derived from the nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation with self-consistent collision structure, demonstrating that quantum statistics manifest at the macroscopic level through modified constants and coefficients in the fluid equations.

title: A spectral-compensated scheme for space-parameter Poisson noise functionals: error bounds and complexity estimates
summary: This paper computes Poisson space noise functionals, $P^{\prime}(u)$, realised in a Gel'fand triple built from a Lévy measure $λ_β(u)du$. We isolate three discretisation parameters: a small-amplitude cut-off, a Donsker delta truncation M, and a chaos order N. For a stable-type intensity $λ_β(u)=cu^{-1-α}$ ($0<α<2$), replacing discarded small amplitudes with matched Gaussian space noise improves the Wasserstein-1 error from $O(ε^{1-α/2})$ to $O(ε)$. The residual is asymptotically normal at $O(ε^{α/2})$. This compensation reduces computational complexity from $O(τ^{-2α/(2-α)})$ to $O(τ^{-α})$. We also evaluate the Gamma-type boundary ($α=0$) and exponential tempering. Truncations converge algebraically (M) and super-geometrically (N). All predicted rates are tightly confirmed by deterministic numerical experiments via Gil-Pelaez inversion, eliminating Monte Carlo noise.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes Poisson space noise functionals P'(u) in a Gel'fand triple based on a Lévy measure, introducing three discretization parameters (amplitude cut-off ε, Donsker delta truncation M, chaos order N). For stable-type intensities, replacing discarded small amplitudes with matched Gaussian noise improves Wasserstein-1 error from O(ε^{1-α/2}) to O(ε), with asymptotically normal residuals at O(ε^{α/2}), reducing computational complexity from O(τ^{-2α/(2-α)}) to O(τ^{-α}). Gamma-type and exponential tempering cases are also analyzed.
AI.motivation: To compute Poisson space noise functionals efficiently by understanding how discretization errors behave and how to compensate for discarded small-amplitude noise contributions using matched Gaussian noise, thereby improving accuracy and reducing computational cost.
AI.method: The paper constructs Poisson space noise functionals in a Gel'fand triple with a Lévy measure λ_β(u)du, isolates three discretization parameters (amplitude cut-off, Donsker delta truncation M, chaos order N), and replaces discarded small-amplitude terms with matched Gaussian space noise to compensate for truncation error. Deterministic numerical verification uses Gil-Pelaez inversion to eliminate Monte Carlo noise.
AI.result: For stable-type intensities (0<α<2), Gaussian compensation improves Wasserstein-1 error from O(ε^{1-α/2}) to O(ε), with asymptotically normal residual at O(ε^{α/2}). Complexity reduces from O(τ^{-2α/(2-α)}) to O(τ^{-α}). Truncation in M converges algebraically and in N super-geometrically. All rates are confirmed numerically.
AI.conclusion: Matched Gaussian compensation of discarded small-amplitude noise is an effective and provably optimal strategy for computing Poisson space noise functionals, achieving first-order accuracy in the cut-off parameter with significant computational savings, verified across stable, Gamma-type, and tempered cases.

title: Variational Formulation of a Hybrid Kinetic and Gyrokinetic Model for Astrophysical and Laboratory Plasmas
summary: We present a Lagrangian model that encapsulates fully kinetic ions and gyrokinetic electrons for solar wind electromagnetic turbulence. Using a consistent method, where both electrons and protons are treated with the same mathematical formalism, we derive and implement a model in which high-frequency waves and kinetic electron effects are described in a computationally cost-efficient way. Higher-order Lie-transform perturbation methods applied to Hamiltonian formulation of guiding center motion are used to describe the dynamics of particles and fields. We use a variational approach to derive field equations for closure of the system.

AI.tldr: A Lagrangian/hybrid model treating ions as fully kinetic and electrons as gyrokinetic is developed for solar wind electromagnetic turbulence, using Lie-transform perturbation methods and a variational approach for field equations.
AI.motivation: To model solar wind electromagnetic turbulence in a computationally efficient way while capturing high-frequency waves and kinetic electron effects that are typically expensive to simulate with fully kinetic approaches.
AI.method: The authors derive a hybrid model with fully kinetic ions and gyrokinetic electrons, treating both species with the same mathematical formalism. They employ higher-order Lie-transform perturbation methods applied to the Hamiltonian formulation of guiding center motion, and use a variational approach to derive field equations for system closure.
AI.result: A consistent, computationally cost-efficient model is derived and implemented that captures high-frequency waves and kinetic electron effects in solar wind turbulence while maintaining a unified mathematical treatment for both particle species.
AI.conclusion: The Lagrangian/hybrid framework provides an efficient and self-consistent approach to simulating solar wind electromagnetic turbulence with kinetic effects from both ions and electrons.

title: Nonlinear Fourier spectral signatures of rogue waves observed in Bose-Einstein condensates
summary: Modulation instability provides an important framework for understanding rogue wave (RW) formation on continuous backgrounds. However, the formation mechanism and nonlinear spectral structures of RWs in Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions remain largely unexplored. Here, we employ the nonlinear Fourier transform (NFT), based on the integrable structure of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the Zakharov-Shabat scattering problem, to investigate two representative classes of first-order RWs in BEC systems. Through nonlinear spectral analysis and Darboux reconstruction, we demonstrate that both Gaussian-wave-packet-induced extreme localization events and experimentally observed Peregrine solitons are governed by the coherent dynamics of discrete soliton modes encoded in the nonlinear spectrum. For Gaussian initial states, increasing the initial width leads to an increasing number of discrete eigenvalues, resulting in a transition from fundamental solitons and bound states to Christmas-tree-like RW structures. For experimentally observed Peregrine solitons, localized perturbations reshape the discrete spectral configuration and phase evolution, enabling coherent focusing of multiple bound soliton modes. Furthermore, we reveal the spectral mechanism of higher-order RWs and propose an inverse spectral-engineering approach based on discrete-spectrum phase matching. Our results provide a nonlinear spectral perspective for understanding and controlling RW formation in matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the nonlinear Fourier transform to analyze rogue wave formation in Bose-Einstein condensate systems with vanishing boundary conditions, showing that both Gaussian-wave-packet-induced extreme events and Peregrine solitons arise from the coherent dynamics of discrete soliton modes in the nonlinear spectrum. The authors propose an inverse spectral-engineering approach for controlling rogue waves.
AI.motivation: While modulation instability explains rogue wave (RW) formation on continuous backgrounds, the formation mechanism and nonlinear spectral structures of RWs in BEC matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors employ the nonlinear Fourier transform (NFT) based on the integrable structure of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the Zakharov-Shabat scattering problem. They analyze two representative classes of first-order RWs through nonlinear spectral analysis and Darboux reconstruction.
AI.result: For Gaussian initial states, increasing the initial width increases the number of discrete eigenvalues, causing a transition from fundamental solitons and bound states to Christmas-tree-like RW structures. For Peregrine solitons, localized perturbations reshape the discrete spectral configuration and phase evolution, enabling coherent focusing of multiple bound soliton modes. They also reveal the spectral mechanism of higher-order RWs.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a nonlinear spectral perspective for understanding and controlling RW formation in matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions, and propose an inverse spectral-engineering approach based on discrete-spectrum phase matching.

title: On The Minkowski Problem With Respect To A Mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Density
summary: In this paper, we pose a new class of Minkowski problems corresponding to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume. Using the flow method, we prove the existence of smooth normalized solutions for the corresponding Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case. Then, by approximation, we obtain the existence of origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new class of Minkowski problems associated with mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume, proves the existence of smooth normalized solutions to the corresponding Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case using a flow method, and then obtains origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem via approximation.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to extend the theory of Minkowski problems to a new setting involving mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume, combining classical Euclidean and Gaussian measures to pose a novel class of geometric problems.
AI.method: The authors use a flow method to prove the existence of smooth normalized solutions for the Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case, followed by an approximation argument to establish the existence of origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem.
AI.result: The paper proves the existence of smooth normalized solutions to the corresponding Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case, and via approximation, establishes the existence of origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully poses and solves a new class of Minkowski problems tied to mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume, providing existence results through both flow and approximation methods.
