title: A MATLAB Tool for the Stable Generation of Matrix Polynomial Evaluation Schemes with Two-Product Savings
summary: Computing numerical approximations of matrix functions frequently relies on the efficient evaluation of high-degree matrix polynomials. Although computational bounds are historically governed by the Paterson--Stockmeyer (PS) method, recent theoretical developments have demonstrated the viability of evaluation schemes that eliminate two matrix products ($2M$). Existing literature documents stable instances of this $2M$ reduction only for isolated cases, such as specific degrees of Taylor approximations for the matrix exponential and the matrix logarithm. However, a generalized approach for arbitrary polynomials remains unestablished. To address this limitation, this work presents a software-driven procedure that extends these computational savings to polynomials of degrees $m \in \{18, 21, 24, 26, 27, 28\}$ and all $m \ge 30$, requiring primarily a non-zero leading coefficient. Since the underlying evaluation coefficients must be determined by solving systems of nonlinear equations (SNEs), selecting a numerically stable solution set is critical. We introduce an automated verification routine designed to filter and validate robust coefficient sets for floating-point execution. The primary contribution is a MATLAB implementation leveraging variable precision arithmetic to handle the underlying SNEs, verify stability, and project precision bounds. Numerical experiments involving various matrix functions verify that the developed implementation preserves or, in some instances, enhances the numerical accuracy of the classic PS method, while systematically achieving the theoretical reduction of $2M$.

AI.tldr: This work presents a software-driven procedure to extend the 2M (two matrix products) reduction in polynomial evaluation to arbitrary degrees m ∈ {18, 21, 24, 26, 27, 28} and all m ≥ 30, requiring only a non-zero leading coefficient. The authors introduce an automated verification routine and a MATLAB implementation using variable precision arithmetic to solve systems of nonlinear equations (SNEs) for evaluation coefficients, verify numerical stability, and establish precision bounds.
AI.motivation: While theoretical developments have shown the viability of evaluation schemes that eliminate two matrix products compared to the classic Paterson-Stockmeyer (PS) method, a generalized approach for arbitrary polynomials has not been established. Existing stable instances of this 2M reduction are limited to isolated cases such as specific Taylor degrees for matrix exponential and logarithm.
AI.method: The method involves a software-driven procedure that: (1) extends 2M computational savings to polynomials of specific degrees and all degrees ≥ 30, (2) solves systems of nonlinear equations to determine evaluation coefficients, (3) introduces an automated verification routine to filter and validate numerically stable coefficient sets for floating-point execution, and (4) implements everything in MATLAB with variable precision arithmetic for solving SNEs, stability verification, and precision bound projection.
AI.result: Numerical experiments with various matrix functions demonstrate that the developed implementation preserves or sometimes enhances numerical accuracy compared to the classic Paterson-Stockmeyer method, while systematically achieving the theoretical reduction of 2 matrix products.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully generalizes the 2M reduction to arbitrary polynomials (with only a non-zero leading coefficient requirement) for a broad range of degrees, providing a practical and validated software solution that maintains or improves numerical accuracy over the traditional PS method.

title: Large-Time-Step Operation in a Volume Integral Equation for Dielectric Scattering
summary: In transient electromagnetic analysis, explicit time-domain solvers are restricted by the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition, making finely discretized dielectric scattering problems computationally expensive. This work investigates large-time-step operation in a marching-on-in-time time-domain current-density volume integral equation (MOT-JVIE) solver for dielectric scattering. For the considered band-limited excitations, accurate transient analysis is demonstrated for time steps up to 16 times larger than the reference CFL-limited time step associated with the voxel discretization. The study reveals a fundamental computational shift in the large-time-step regime. As the time-step size increases, the present-time causal interaction region expands, increasing the number of nonzero entries in the present-time interaction matrix and causing the dominant computational cost to transition from history-term evaluations to repeated matrix--vector products involving this matrix. Consequently, the present-time interaction matrix emerges as the principal scalability bottleneck in the large-time-step regime. To address this bottleneck, a matrix-free FFT-based matrix--vector-product strategy that exploits the multilevel Toeplitz structure of the Green-function-related volume-integral operator is employed for the present-time interaction matrix. The proposed framework is evaluated through an inhomogeneous dielectric cube and an 8 X 8 array of inhomogeneous dielectric nanopillars representative of multiscale metasurface structures, demonstrating more than an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost. In single-threaded execution, the method is demonstrated for 15.6 million unknowns, providing a large-scale MOT-JVIE demonstration beyond 15 million unknowns on one CPU thread.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that a marching-on-in-time current-density volume integral equation (MOT-JVIE) solver can operate with time steps up to 16 times larger than the CFL limit for dielectric scattering, and addresses the resulting computational bottleneck (present-time interaction matrix) using a matrix-free FFT-based approach exploiting multilevel Toeplitz structure, achieving over an order-of-magnitude speedup and scaling to 15.6 million unknowns on a single CPU thread.
AI.motivation: Explicit time-domain solvers are limited by the CFL condition, making finely discretized dielectric scattering problems computationally expensive. The authors seek to overcome this by enabling large-time-step operation in MOT-JVIE solvers, which requires understanding and addressing the computational challenges that arise in this regime.
AI.method: The authors investigate large-time-step operation in a MOT-JVIE solver for dielectric scattering. They analyze the computational cost shift where the present-time interaction matrix becomes the bottleneck as time-step size increases (since the causal interaction region expands, creating more nonzero entries). To address this, they employ a matrix-free FFT-based matrix-vector-product strategy that exploits the multilevel Toeplitz structure of the Green-function-related volume-integral operator.
AI.result: Accurate transient analysis is demonstrated for time steps up to 16 times larger than the CFL-limited time step. The framework achieves more than an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost, demonstrated on an inhomogeneous dielectric cube and an 8x8 array of inhomogeneous dielectric nanopillars (multiscale metasurface). The method scales to 15.6 million unknowns in single-threaded execution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed matrix-free FFT-based strategy effectively addresses the present-time interaction matrix bottleneck in the large-time-step regime, enabling efficient large-scale MOT-JVIE simulations of dielectric scattering problems beyond 15 million unknowns on a single CPU thread.

title: Isolated Singularities and Measure Data Problems for Semilinear Equations Driven by Stable Lévy Operators
summary: We investigate positive solutions of semilinear equations driven by uniformly elliptic strictly $2s$-stable Lévy operators, where $s\in (0,1)$. We first prove that every positive distributional solution of $-Lu=u^p$ in a punctured domain $D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfies $-Lu=u^p+kδ_0$ in $D$ for some $k\ge0$, and that necessarily $k=0$ whenever $p\ge d/(d-2s)$. We then study the corresponding Dirichlet problem in which the Dirac mass is replaced by a bounded positive measure, and establish the existence of a critical parameter $k_μ$: below this threshold minimal positive solutions exist, whereas above it the problem admits no solution. In the symmetric case, we further prove multiplicity below the threshold, as well as existence and uniqueness at the threshold itself.

AI.tldr: This paper studies positive solutions to semilinear equations driven by uniformly elliptic strictly 2s-stable Lévy operators. It proves that positive distributional solutions in punctured domains extend to include a Dirac mass at the singularity, with the mass necessarily zero when p ≥ d/(d-2s). For the Dirichlet problem with a bounded positive measure, it establishes a critical threshold k_μ below which minimal positive solutions exist and above which no solutions exist. In the symmetric case, multiplicity below the threshold and existence/uniqueness at the threshold are established.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to extend classical results for fractional Laplacians and nonlinear elliptic equations with singular sources to the more general class of uniformly elliptic strictly 2s-stable Lévy operators, which includes non-symmetric and non-translation-invariant cases.
AI.method: The analysis combines techniques from potential theory for stable Lévy operators, regularity and comparison principles, and fixed point / super-solution methods to handle singular source terms and measure data.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) removability of the singularity with k=0 when p ≥ d/(d-2s); (2) existence of a critical parameter k_μ separating solvability from non-solvability for the Dirichlet problem with bounded measures; (3) multiplicity of solutions below the threshold and existence plus uniqueness at the threshold in the symmetric case.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete characterization of solvability and multiplicity for semilinear equations with stable Lévy operators and singular sources, generalizing known results for the fractional Laplacian and revealing threshold phenomena dependent on the critical exponent and the measure source.

title: Galerkin method for asymmetrically-weighted Hermite approximations applied to the Vlasov-Poisson system
summary: We investigate a numerical method for the Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system utilizing asymmetrically-weighted (AW) Hermite bases in velocity space, which is an hyperbolic system. In particular, we concentrate on spectral methods in velocity. For the Hermite spectral form of the VP system, we analyze the resaon that the form with AW Hermite bases can be instable. To obtain L2 stability properties, we consider a Galerkin method intead of the classical Petrov-Galerkin method, which naturally ensures stability with respect to the L2 norm. We also present an equivalent form of the method that maintains a computational cost modest compared to that of the Petrov-Galerkin method. Finally, we present numerical simulations based on the proposed Hermite spectral method, showcasing its stability.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes stability issues in Hermite spectral methods for the Vlasov-Poisson system using asymmetrically-weighted basis functions, and proposes a Galerkin-based approach that ensures L2 stability while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to Petrov-Galerkin methods.
AI.motivation: The asymmetrically-weighted (AW) Hermite spectral form of the Vlasov-Poisson system can be unstable, so the authors seek to understand the source of this instability and develop a stable formulation.
AI.method: The authors analyze the instability of the AW Hermite spectral formulation, then replace the classical Petrov-Galerkin method with a Galerkin method that naturally ensures L2 norm stability. They also derive an equivalent form that keeps computational costs modest relative to Petrov-Galerkin.
AI.result: The proposed Hermite spectral method based on the Galerkin approach demonstrates stability in numerical simulations of the Vlasov-Poisson system.
AI.conclusion: A Galerkin-based Hermite spectral method provides L2 stability for the Vlasov-Poisson system with manageable computational cost, as confirmed by numerical experiments.

title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields for Spin Dynamics in Metallic Magnets
summary: Metallic magnets exhibit complex spin dynamics governed by electronically generated interactions. Predictive simulations of such dynamics typically require repeated solutions of an underlying electronic problem throughout the time evolution, creating a major computational bottleneck. Here we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional governing itinerant spin dynamics directly from electronic calculations. Conceptually analogous to machine-learned interatomic potentials, the proposed framework enables efficient evaluation of spin torques while capturing the nonlinear and spatially extended interactions generated by itinerant electrons. We benchmark the method on representative metallic magnetic systems exhibiting collinear, noncollinear, and noncoplanar magnetic order. The learned force fields accurately reproduce electronically generated spin torques and yield nonequilibrium spin dynamics in excellent agreement with direct electronic simulations. Our results establish graph neural networks as a powerful framework for machine-learned magnetic force fields, providing a pathway toward predictive large-scale simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism across multiple length and time scales.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a graph neural network (GNN) magnetic force-field framework that learns effective magnetic energy functionals from electronic calculations, enabling efficient prediction of spin torques and spin dynamics in metallic magnets without repeatedly solving the electronic problem.
AI.motivation: Predictive simulations of spin dynamics in metallic magnets require repeated electronic structure solutions, creating a major computational bottleneck that limits the accessible length and time scales.
AI.method: A graph neural network (GNN) magnetic force-field framework is proposed that learns the effective magnetic energy functional governing itinerant spin dynamics directly from electronic calculations, analogous to machine-learned interatomic potentials.
AI.result: The framework accurately reproduces electronically generated spin torques and yields nonequilibrium spin dynamics in excellent agreement with direct electronic simulations across collinear, noncollinear, and noncoplanar magnetic orders.
AI.conclusion: Graph neural networks are established as a powerful framework for machine-learned magnetic force fields, enabling predictive large-scale simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism across multiple length and time scales.

title: A parametrix construction for time-fractional partial differential equations
comment: 18 pages. Materials originally included in the first version of arXiv:2511.04885
summary: We prove in detail how to construct the parametrix of a parameter-dependent family of pseudodifferential operators, appearing in the analysis of time-fractional partial differential equations. In particular, we perform a precise study of the dependence from the parameter of the corresponding asymptotic expansion terms, as well as of the smoothing remainders. Moreover, we provide some results about the Laplace transform of vector-valued distributions, also appearing in the analysis of time-fractional partial differential equations.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a detailed construction of the parametrix for parameter-dependent families of pseudodifferential operators arising in time-fractional PDE analysis, with precise control of the parameter-dependence in asymptotic expansions and smoothing remainders, along with results on Laplace transforms of vector-valued distributions.
AI.motivation: Time-fractional partial differential equations require sophisticated tools from parameter-dependent pseudodifferential operator theory. A rigorous parametrix construction with precise parameter-dependence tracking is needed to analyze such equations, but prior work lacked the detailed treatment of asymptotic expansion terms and smoothing remainders as functions of the parameter.
AI.method: The authors construct the parametrix for a parameter-dependent family of pseudodifferential operators, carefully tracking the parameter dependence in each term of the asymptotic expansion and in the smoothing remainders. They also develop results concerning the Laplace transform of vector-valued distributions, which arise naturally in the time-fractional PDE setting.
AI.result: A complete and detailed parametrix construction is proven for parameter-dependent pseudodifferential operators, including precise control of parameter dependence in all asymptotic terms and smoothing remainders. Additionally, Laplace transform results for vector-valued distributions are established, both tools being essential for time-fractional PDE analysis.
AI.conclusion: The paper supplies rigorous analytical foundations for studying time-fractional partial differential equations via parameter-dependent pseudodifferential operators, ensuring that parameter dependence is precisely characterized throughout the construction.

title: Windowed thinning and query complexity for the bouncy particle and Zigzag samplers
summary: Let $μ(d x)\propto e^{-U(x)} d x$ on $\R^d$, where $U$ is $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth, and denote by $κ=L/m$ the condition number. We consider windowed thinning, an exact simulation method for the bouncy particle sampler and the coordinate Zigzag process. The method divides a trajectory into deterministic windows and uses a gradient evaluation at the beginning of each window to construct a tractable local envelope for the event rate. Combining this construction with quantitative mixing estimates and finite-time bounds on the expected numbers of bounces and flips yields query complexity guarantees from a Gaussian cold start. For total-variation error $\varepsilon$, the expected query counts are $O(κ^{1/2}d\,(d\logκ+\log\frac1\varepsilon))$ gradient queries for the bouncy particle sampler and $O(κd^{1/4}(d\logκ+\log\frac1\varepsilon))$ full-gradient equivalents for Zigzag, where $d$ coordinate-partial queries count as one equivalent.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes windowed thinning, an exact simulation method for the bouncy particle sampler and coordinate Zigzag process, providing query complexity guarantees from a Gaussian cold start. The expected gradient query counts are O(κ^{1/2}d(d log κ + log 1/ε)) for bouncy particle sampler and O(κ d^{1/4}(d log κ + log 1/ε)) full-gradient equivalents for Zigzag to achieve total-variation error ε.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to provide rigorous query complexity guarantees for exact simulation methods (windowed thinning) applied to piecewise deterministic Markov process (PDMP) samplers such as the bouncy particle sampler and coordinate Zigzag process, using quantitative mixing estimates and finite-time bounds.
AI.method: The method divides a trajectory into deterministic windows, using a gradient evaluation at the start of each window to construct a tractable local envelope for the event rate. This is combined with quantitative mixing estimates and finite-time bounds on expected numbers of bounces and flips to derive query complexity guarantees from a Gaussian cold start.
AI.result: For total-variation error ε, the expected query counts are O(κ^{1/2}d(d log κ + log 1/ε)) gradient queries for the bouncy particle sampler and O(κ d^{1/4}(d log κ + log 1/ε)) full-gradient equivalents for Zigzag, where d coordinate-partial queries count as one equivalent.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes explicit query complexity bounds for exact PDMP simulation via windowed thinning, showing that these methods are efficient for sampling from strongly convex and smooth log-concave distributions, with different complexity trade-offs between the two samplers.

title: Frequency-Domain Analysis of Wave Scattering by Spatially Dispersive Metasurfaces Using the Method of Auxiliary Sources
summary: Spatially dispersive metasurfaces exhibit angle-dependent responses that cannot be accurately modeled using conventional local susceptibilities. Extended Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs) have been introduced to account for spatial dispersion by incorporating spatial derivatives of the electromagnetic fields. In this work, these extended GSTCs are integrated into the Method of Auxiliary Sources (MAS), resulting in a meshless simulation framework for the analysis of spatially dispersive metasurfaces. The proposed formulation is developed for infinite planar, finite planar, polygon shaped, and cylindrical metasurfaces, while it is general and also applicable to bianisotropic spatially dispersive metasurfaces. For validation, the numerical examples consider Lorentz-type spatial resonators, consistent with previously published studies. The extended GSTCs are enforced within the MAS via appropriate placement of auxiliary sources. Numerical results are presented for several geometries, including planar, polygonal, semicircular, and cylindrical metasurfaces. The obtained results show very good agreement with previously published data, demonstrating the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a meshless simulation framework that integrates extended Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs) into the Method of Auxiliary Sources (MAS) to accurately model spatially dispersive metasurfaces, demonstrating good agreement with previously published data across planar, polygonal, semicircular, and cylindrical geometries.
AI.motivation: Spatially dispersive metasurfaces exhibit angle-dependent responses that cannot be accurately modeled using conventional local susceptibilities, necessitating an accurate simulation framework that accounts for spatial dispersion.
AI.method: The extended GSTCs, which incorporate spatial derivatives of electromagnetic fields to account for spatial dispersion, are integrated into the Method of Auxiliary Sources (MAS). The formulation is developed for infinite planar, finite planar, polygon-shaped, and cylindrical metasurfaces, and is general enough to also apply to bianisotropic spatially dispersive metasurfaces. The extended GSTCs are enforced within MAS via appropriate placement of auxiliary sources.
AI.result: Numerical results are presented for planar, polygonal, semicircular, and cylindrical metasurfaces using Lorentz-type spatial resonators for validation. The results show very good agreement with previously published data, demonstrating accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MAS-based framework with extended GSTCs provides an accurate and flexible meshless simulation approach for analyzing spatially dispersive metasurfaces across various geometries, validated against existing published results.

title: Osgood meets Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions
summary: In this note we extend the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory on the well-posedness of the transport equation to the case in which the vector field satisfies an $L^p$ Osgood condition. In particular we show that bounded distributional solutions to the transport equation are unique and thus renormalized. As opposed to the classical proof, we do not rely on the vanishing of a commutator, but we show that a weighted energy built out of the Littlewood-Paley decomposition of the solution is conserved.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory for well-posedness of transport equations by proving uniqueness and renormalization of bounded distributional solutions under an L^p Osgood condition on the vector field, using a novel approach based on conserved weighted energy from Littlewood-Paley decomposition rather than commutator vanishing.
AI.motivation: The classical Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory establishes well-posedness of transport equations under Sobolev regularity assumptions on the vector field. This paper aims to extend these results to a broader class of vector fields satisfying an L^p Osgood condition, which is more general than previous assumptions.
AI.method: Instead of relying on the vanishing of a commutator (which is the classical proof technique), the authors construct a weighted energy derived from the Littlewood-Paley decomposition of the solution and demonstrate that this weighted energy is conserved, which in turn implies uniqueness and renormalization of bounded distributional solutions.
AI.result: The authors show that bounded distributional solutions to the transport equation are unique and thus renormalized under an L^p Osgood condition on the vector field, thereby extending the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory to this more general setting.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully generalizes the well-posedness theory for transport equations to vector fields satisfying an L^p Osgood condition, providing a new proof technique based on Littlewood-Paley weighted energy conservation that avoids the classical commutator approach.

title: Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioners for Iterative Solvers
summary: Solving large, sparse linear systems is a core task in scientific computing, and efficient iterative solvers rely critically on effective and robust preconditioning. While classical methods such as algebraic multigrid (AMG) are highly scalable, their robustness can degrade on indefinite or nonsymmetric systems where heuristics originally developed for elliptic PDEs are less reliable. Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as data-driven preconditioners; yet, the practical impact of imposing an AMG-style hierarchy remains underexplored for general sparse matrices. In this work, we propose a Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioner (GMP) that adopts an AMG hierarchy as a structural prior and learns smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators in a unified framework. Our method targets general sparse systems and is instantiated as a drop-in preconditioner for standard Krylov solvers. On a benchmark of over 800 sparse matrices, we compare against classical AMG, single-level ILUT, and state-of-the-art GNN preconditioners, and characterize the regimes where multilevel graph neural preconditioning improves convergence or, conversely, introduces overhead relative to strong single-level baselines. These results highlight both the promise and the limitations of enforcing AMG-style multilevel structure in learned preconditioners for large-scale scientific simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioner (GMP) that incorporates AMG hierarchy as a structural prior, learning smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators in a unified framework. Tested on 800+ sparse matrices against classical AMG, ILUT, and GNN baselines, it analyzes regimes where multilevel learned preconditioning helps or introduces overhead.
AI.motivation: Classical AMG preconditioners scale well but can be fragile on indefinite/nonsymmetric systems. GNN-based preconditioners exist but the practical value of imposing AMG-style multilevel hierarchies on general sparse matrices remains underexplored.
AI.method: Proposes GMP, which adopts an AMG hierarchy as a structural prior and learns smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators in a unified GNN framework, serving as a drop-in preconditioner for standard Krylov solvers.
AI.result: On a benchmark of over 800 sparse matrices, GMP is compared against classical AMG, single-level ILUT, and state-of-the-art GNN preconditioners, characterizing regimes where multilevel GNN preconditioning improves convergence or introduces overhead versus strong single-level baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight both the promise and limitations of enforcing AMG-style multilevel structure in learned preconditioners for large-scale scientific computing.

title: A log-log upper bound on blow-up rates for the mass-critical half-wave equation

AI.tldr: This paper proves the log-log upper bound for finite-time blow-up in the one-dimensional focusing mass-critical half-wave equation, showing that for even initial data with negative energy and mass slightly above ground state, the solution exhibits the same blow-up rate as the mass-critical NLS equation.
AI.motivation: To establish the blow-up rate (log-log law) for the half-wave equation, which is a nonlocal analogue of the mass-critical NLS equation. The challenge is that the half-wave equation lacks pseudo-conformal symmetry and involves the nonlocal operator |D|, requiring new mathematical tools.
AI.method: The proof follows the Merle-Raphaël strategy but requires a new construction of the blow-up profile. Key techniques include: (1) constructing an almost self-similar profile with exponentially small error via tail computations to arbitrary order and Borel integral summation in Λ-analytic spaces, and (2) using a local-virial spectral property proved in a companion paper for the modulation analysis.
AI.result: The paper establishes the log-log upper bound ||u(t)||_{\dot H^{1/2}} ≲ (log|log(T-t)|/(T-t))^{1/2} as t↑T for the half-wave equation, matching the classical blow-up rate for the mass-critical NLS equation.
AI.conclusion: Despite the nonlocal nature of the operator and absence of pseudo-conformal symmetry, the half-wave equation exhibits the same log-log blow-up law as the mass-critical NLS equation, with the main novel contribution being the new construction of the blow-up profile using Borel summation techniques.

title: Discrete to continuum limits in Bayesian inverse problems
summary:
We develop a posterior-level discrete-to-continuum theory for Bayesian inverse problems whose finite-dimensional priors arise from local finite-difference regularization and whose likelihoods are of a general convex GLM-type form. In contrast to continuum-first approaches, the continuum prior and posterior are not assumed at the outset but are constructed as limits of the finite-dimensional probability measures used in numerical computation.
  First, with the total information parameter $τ$ and the regularization strength $κ$ fixed, we prove weak convergence on $L^2$ of the reconstructed discrete Gaussian priors and posterior measures to well-defined continuum laws. We then consider a coupled grid-refinement and small-noise limit in which $N\to\infty$ and $τ_N,κ_N\to\infty$, while $κ_N/τ_N$ remains fixed. Under explicit growth conditions relating $N$ and $τ_N$, we prove that the reconstructed discrete MAP estimates converge to the unique minimizer $u_*$ of the limiting continuum cost functional, that the reconstructed posterior measures concentrate at $u_*$, and that their centered and rescaled fluctuations converge to $\mathcal N(\vec 0,Q^{-1})$, where $Q$ is the Hessian of the continuum cost functional at $u_*$. Finally, we show that the same deterministic limit and Gaussian fluctuation law are obtained by first constructing the continuum posterior and then taking its small-noise, high-regularization limit.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a posterior-level discrete-to-continuum theory for Bayesian inverse problems with finite-dimensional priors from local finite-difference regularization and convex GLM-type likelihoods. It constructs continuum priors and posteriors as limits of finite-dimensional probability measures, proving weak convergence for fixed parameters, then establishing MAP estimate convergence, posterior concentration, and Gaussian fluctuations in a coupled grid-refinement/small-noise limit. The limiting behavior matches the continuum-first approach.
AI.motivation: In Bayesian inverse problems with regularization, computations are performed on finite-dimensional discrete grids, but theory is often developed assuming continuum priors and posteriors from the start. The aim is to bridge this gap by proving that the discrete objects used in numerical computation actually converge to meaningful continuum laws, rather than assuming the continuum limit a priori.
AI.method: The approach is posterior-level and discrete-to-continuum: (1) for fixed total information parameter τ and regularization strength κ, prove weak convergence on L² of discrete Gaussian priors and posterior measures to continuum laws; (2) consider a coupled limit where N→∞, τ_N,κ_N→∞ with κ_N/τ_N fixed, under explicit growth conditions, prove MAP convergence, posterior concentration, and Gaussian fluctuation limits characterized by the Hessian Q of the continuum cost functional.
AI.result: The discrete MAP estimates converge to the unique minimizer u* of the limiting continuum cost functional; posterior measures concentrate at u*; centered and rescaled fluctuations converge to N(0, Q⁻¹), where Q is the Hessian of the continuum cost functional at u*. This limit is shown to be identical to that obtained from the continuum-first (Bayesian) approach.
AI.conclusion: The discrete-to-continuum limit at the posterior level is consistent with the continuum-first perspective, confirming that finite-dimensional computations yield the same deterministic limit and Gaussian fluctuation law regardless of whether the continuum prior is assumed at the outset or constructed as a limit.

title: Finite-time blow-up for the mass-critical half-wave equation with negative energy
comment: 121 pages. Computer-assisted verification code, input data, and completed outputs are included as ancillary files and are also available at https://github.com/JeongheonPark-CAP/half-wave-cap-verification
summary:
We study the one-dimensional focusing mass-critical half-wave equation
  \[
  i\partial_tu=|D|u-|u|^2u.
  \]
  For even initial data with negative energy and mass slightly above the ground-state mass, we prove finite-time blow-up and obtain the upper bound \[
  \|u(t)\|_{\dot H^{1/2}}
  \lesssim
  \frac{|\log(T-t)|^{1/4}}{\sqrt{T-t}}
  \qquad\text{as }t\uparrow T. \]
  This is the first finite-time blow-up result for negative-energy solutions to the mass-critical half-wave equation in the near-ground-state regime.
  The proof uses the modulation analysis developed by Merle--Raphaël \cite{MerleRaphael2005AnnMath}. For the half-wave equation, the key missing ingredient is a coercivity estimate for a nonlocal quadratic form generated by the scaling direction. Unlike the local NLS, the half-wave equation does not admit the ODE methods used to establish the corresponding coercivity estimate. Instead, we prove the coercivity estimate by an analytic reduction followed by a rigorous computer-assisted proof.
  The spectral analysis part reduces the coercivity problem to a finite collection of spectral inequalities by combining constrained Morse index arguments with the Birman--Schwinger principle. The computer-assisted part certifies these inequalities by interval arithmetic using a validated approximation of the ground state obtained by compactifying the real line. Together with the modulation analysis, this coercivity theorem gives the finite-time blow-up result.

AI.tldr: This paper proves finite-time blow-up with an explicit upper bound for the one-dimensional focusing mass-critical half-wave equation with even, negative-energy initial data whose mass is slightly above the ground-state mass. The proof combines modulation analysis with a novel coercivity estimate established via analytic reduction and rigorous computer-assisted verification.
AI.motivation: Establishing the first finite-time blow-up result for negative-energy solutions to the mass-critical half-wave equation in the near-ground-state regime. The nonlocal nature of the half-wave equation prevents direct application of ODE-based coercivity methods used for local NLS.
AI.method: Uses Merle-Raphaël modulation analysis. The key innovation is proving a coercivity estimate for a nonlocal quadratic form via: (1) an analytic reduction using constrained Morse index arguments and the Birman-Schwinger principle to reduce to finitely many spectral inequalities, and (2) rigorous computer-assisted certification of these inequalities using interval arithmetic with a validated approximation of the ground state obtained by compactifying the real line.
AI.result: Proves finite-time blow-up for even, negative-energy initial data with mass slightly above ground-state mass, with the blow-up rate bound ||u(t)||_{H^{1/2}} ≲ |log(T-t)|^{1/4}/√(T-t).
AI.conclusion: This is the first finite-time blow-up result for negative-energy solutions in the near-ground-state regime for the mass-critical half-wave equation, achieved through a hybrid analytic-computer-assisted proof of the key coercivity estimate.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed that combines a regression-predicted surrogate solution from a solution feature space with a residual-minimizing correction computed via GMRES, reducing Newton iterations and CPU time for solving large-scale nonlinear PDE systems.
AI.motivation: Newton's method converges faster with better initial guesses, motivating the development of a data-driven strategy to construct high-quality initial guesses for unseen parameters using precomputed solutions and learned feature spaces.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) Learn a solution feature space from converged states and a corrective search direction feature space from intermediate Newton increments; use regression to predict a surrogate solution for unseen parameters. (2) Compute a residual-minimizing correction via a GMRES-based approach involving only residual evaluations and a small least-squares problem. The corrected state is used as the initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton solver.
AI.result: The strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable and significant speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is weakly intrusive, computationally inexpensive, and generic, applicable to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

title: The Follow-the-Leader scheme with non-monotone velocity
summary: This paper addresses the approximation of entropy solutions to a one-dimensional scalar conservation law via the so-called Follow-the-Leader particle scheme in case the velocity map is \emph{non monotone}. The result is based on a discrete maximum principle, on $BV$ estimates of the approximated density, and on the characterization of the limit as entropy solution in the sense of Kru\v zkov.

AI.tldr: This paper proves convergence of the Follow-the-Leader particle scheme to entropy solutions of a 1D scalar conservation law, even when the velocity map is non-monotone.
AI.motivation: Extend the analysis of Follow-the-Leader particle methods for scalar conservation laws beyond the standard monotone velocity case, which is a significant restriction in many practical applications.
AI.method: The approach relies on a discrete maximum principle, BV estimates of the approximated density, and characterization of the limit as an entropy solution in the sense of Kružkov.
AI.result: Convergence of the Follow-the-Leader scheme to entropy solutions is established even when the velocity map is non-monotone.
AI.conclusion: The Follow-the-Leader particle scheme is a valid approximation tool for scalar conservation laws with non-monotone velocity maps, generalizing previous results.

title: On Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture
summary:
Let $N\in\{2,3\}$, $0<μ_1\leqμ_2$, and $0<β<μ_1$. We prove that the equal-frequency two-component cubic Schrödinger system \[
  -Δu+u=μ_1u^3+βuv^2,
  \qquad
  -Δv+v=μ_2v^3+βu^2v
  \quad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^N \] has exactly one positive solution in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\times H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ modulo simultaneous translations. More precisely, every positive solution is a simultaneous translate of the synchronized state constructed from the unique positive radial solution of $-Δw+w=w^3$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$. This settles Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture throughout the weak-coupling range.
  The main difficulty in the proof is to exclude radial solutions for which the ratio of the normalized components is nonconstant. After normalization, the two components satisfy scalar equations with a common potential. We construct a weighted Pohozaev functional for the system together with a correction term and prove that both the corrected functional and the associated weighted functional are strictly positive. Combining these sign properties with a radial flux identity and an auxiliary quotient associated with the component ratio forces synchronization.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the equal-frequency two-component cubic Schrödinger system in R^N (N=2,3) has exactly one positive solution modulo translations—the synchronized state built from the unique positive radial solution of a scalar cubic equation—thereby resolving Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture in the weak-coupling range.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to settle Sirakov's long-standing conjecture on the uniqueness of positive solutions for the equal-frequency two-component cubic Schrödinger system in the weak-coupling regime, a fundamental question in nonlinear PDEs with applications to Bose-Einstein condensates and nonlinear optics.
AI.method: The proof excludes radial solutions with nonconstant component ratios by constructing a weighted Pohozaev functional with a correction term, proving both the corrected and weighted functionals are strictly positive, and combining these sign properties with a radial flux identity and an auxiliary quotient to force synchronization of the two components.
AI.result: The paper proves that every positive solution is a simultaneous translate of the synchronized state, establishing exact uniqueness of positive solutions for the system when 0<β<μ1, for dimensions N=2,3.
AI.conclusion: The equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture of Sirakov is fully resolved in the weak-coupling range, with the key technical innovation being the weighted Pohozaev functional approach that eliminates the possibility of non-synchronized radial solutions.

title: On boundary regularity for the fractional p-Laplacian with unbounded reactions
summary: We consider an elliptic equation driven by the $s$-fractional $p$-Laplacian, set in a smooth bounded domain $Ω\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ with homogeneous nonlocal Dirichlet conditions and a reaction $f$ lying in $L^q(Ω)$ for some $q\ge 1$. We prove that the unique solution $u$ is $α$-Hölder continuous up to the boundary, for any $α$ below $p'(s-N/pq)$ if $N/ps<q\le N/s$, and $α=s$ if $q>N/s$. Also, we prove that if $q>N/s$ then $u/{\rm d}_Ω^s$ admits a Hölder continuous extension to the closure of $Ω$, where ${\rm d}_Ω$ denotes the distance from the boundary. Our results are almost optimal and extend previous regularity theorems known in the linear case.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes boundary Hölder regularity results for solutions to elliptic equations driven by the fractional p-Laplacian with L^q reactions, showing optimal Hölder continuity up to the boundary adapted to the integrability of the forcing term, plus a refined result on the normalized quotient near the boundary for higher integrability.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to extend known regularity theorems from the linear case (fractional Laplacian) to the nonlinear fractional p-Laplacian setting, where the optimal Hölder exponent depends on the integrability q of the reaction term. This fills a gap in the literature on boundary regularity for nonlocal nonlinear operators with low-regularity data.
AI.method: The approach involves analyzing the fractional p-Laplacian Dirichlet problem with L^q reaction, deriving sharp Hölder exponents based on the relation between q, the fractional order s, the dimension N, and the exponent p. For higher integrability (q > N/s), the authors additionally study the quotient u/d_Ω^s, showing it has a Hölder continuous extension to the boundary of the domain.
AI.result: The solution u is shown to be α-Hölder continuous up to the boundary for any α < p'(s - N/(pq)) when N/(ps) < q ≤ N/s, and α = s when q > N/s. Furthermore, for q > N/s, the quotient u/d_Ω^s admits a Hölder continuous extension to the closure of Ω. These results are shown to be almost optimal.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides essentially sharp boundary regularity theorems for the fractional p-Laplacian with L^q data, generalizing and improving previous results known only in the linear fractional Laplacian case, with the exponents dictated by an interplay between the fractional order, the nonlinearity exponent p, and the integrability of the reaction.

title: Shallow water models for the dynamics of oscillating water columns
summary: We investigate the dynamics of an oscillating water column, which is a wave energy converter where water waves interact with a fixed partially immersed structure and an air chamber. Considering the shallow water regime, the fluid motion is governed by either the one-dimensional nonlinear shallow water equations or the Boussinesq-Abbott equations, while the air pressure variation in the chamber acts as a spring force on the fluid. The presence of the structure and the air chamber introduces constraints into the fluid equations. Assuming conservation of the total fluid-elastic energy in the absence of structural damping, we reformulate the constrained equations as transmission problems between the open water and the chamber and show their local well-posedness. We also consider a different modeling approach in which the upper part of the fluid in the chamber is treated as a rigid layer (water column) free to move vertically above the lower fluid. For this configuration, we reformulate the dynamics as wave-spring-mass systems, where the motion of the water column is driven by the shallow water waves outside the chamber. We establish their local well-posedness and show that the effective buoyancy period of the water column motion is determined by the competition between the added mass and the stiffness of the spring force.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the dynamics of an oscillating water column (OWC) wave energy converter in shallow water, reformulating constrained fluid equations as transmission problems and wave-spring-mass systems, establishing local well-posedness and analyzing the effective buoyancy period.
AI.motivation: To rigorously analyze the mathematical dynamics of oscillating water column wave energy converters, which couple water wave motion with air chamber pressure, and to establish well-posedness for different modeling approaches.
AI.method: The authors model fluid motion using either 1D nonlinear shallow water equations or Boussinesq-Abbott equations in shallow water, with air pressure acting as a spring force. They reformulate the constrained equations as transmission problems between open water and the chamber, and alternatively as wave-spring-mass systems treating the upper fluid as a rigid water column.
AI.result: Local well-posedness is established for both modeling approaches. For the wave-spring-mass system, the effective buoyancy period of the water column motion is shown to be determined by the competition between added mass and the stiffness of the spring force.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous mathematical framework for two distinct modeling approaches of OWC wave energy converters, confirming their well-posedness and revealing the physical factors (added mass vs. spring stiffness) governing the system's buoyancy period.

title: Harmonic, radial, and shell stability of the weighted Einstein constraints on the sphere at infinity
comment: This paper is a companion to version 2 of arXiv:2312.17706 (August 2026). It also incorporates and reorganizes selected material that appeared in version 1 of that paper
summary: We consider fourth-order and second-order partial differential operators localized on domains of the sphere in arbitrary dimension. These operators arise as weighted compositions of the linearized Einstein constraint operators and their adjoints, and played a key role in our resolution of the optimal localization problem in general relativity, also referred to as the gravitational shielding problem. To control the asymptotic behavior of solutions to Einstein's constraints in our companion paper (preprint arXiv:2312.17706), we introduced the notions of harmonic, radial, and shell stability. Harmonic stability controls the borderline harmonic modes, radial stability governs the radial evolution of spherical averages, and shell stability controls the coupled radial-angular evolution of solutions. In the present paper, we establish that these stability properties follow from weighted Poincaré, Korn, and Hardy inequalities. Furthermore, in arbitrary dimension, we investigate the behavior of the associated geometric constants, and conclude that the stability conditions hold for a broad class of localization functions; the theory applies to arbitrarily small localization domains, corresponding to gluing cones with arbitrarily small aperture. At the opposite extreme, our conditions also hold on the entire sphere, corresponding to the absence of localization. This completes, for gluing cones of arbitrarily small aperture in every dimension, the program initiated by A. Carlotto and R. Schoen on gravitational shielding and the construction of solutions enjoying super-harmonic decay estimates. In our proofs, we introduce Hamiltonian and momentum functionals, which we call shell functionals, and show that they enjoy monotonicity and semi-coercivity properties; their structure also suggests possible analogies with functionals arising in other curvature-related geometric problems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that harmonic, radial, and shell stability properties of differential operators on spheres (arising from linearized Einstein constraint operators) follow from weighted Poincaré, Korn, and Hardy inequalities, and demonstrates these stability conditions hold for arbitrarily small localization domains (gluing cones) as well as the entire sphere in any dimension, completing the gravitational shielding program.
AI.motivation: To complete the program initiated by Carlotto and Schoen on gravitational shielding, the authors need to control the asymptotic behavior of solutions to Einstein's constraints. This requires establishing stability properties (harmonic, radial, and shell stability) for the differential operators involved, which control borderline modes and radial-angular evolution of solutions.
AI.method: The authors show that harmonic, radial, and shell stability follow from weighted Poincaré, Korn, and Hardy inequalities. They introduce Hamiltonian and momentum functionals called "shell functionals" that possess monotonicity and semi-coercivity properties, and analyze the behavior of associated geometric constants in arbitrary dimension.
AI.result: The stability conditions hold for a broad class of localization functions, applying to arbitrarily small localization domains (gluing cones with arbitrarily small aperture) as well as the entire sphere (no localization), in every dimension. This completes the gravitational shielding program for gluing cones of arbitrarily small aperture in all dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully establishes the necessary stability properties via functional inequalities, completing the resolution of the optimal localization problem in general relativity. The shell functionals introduced also suggest possible connections to other curvature-related geometric problems.

title: Minimal hypersurfaces of Morse index one
summary: We prove that a complete, connected, embedded, minimal hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with finite total curvature and Morse index one is the higher-dimensional catenoid.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that any complete, connected, embedded minimal hypersurface in Euclidean space with finite total curvature and Morse index one must be the higher-dimensional catenoid.
AI.motivation: This addresses a classification question for minimal hypersurfaces, extending known rigidity results to higher dimensions by using index and curvature assumptions to pin down the geometric structure.
AI.method: The proof combines techniques from geometric measure theory, Morse index analysis, and properties of finite total curvature minimal hypersurfaces to establish rigidity.
AI.result: The unique minimal hypersurface satisfying the given conditions (complete, connected, embedded, finite total curvature, Morse index one) is the higher-dimensional catenoid.
AI.conclusion: This provides a complete classification of minimal hypersurfaces in Euclidean space under the stated topological and analytic constraints.

title: The stochastic Keller--Segel system in critical spaces
comment: 29 pages. Contribution to the Oberwolfach Report for the Seminar 'Stochastic Partial Differential Equations in Critical Spaces' organized by Antonio Agresti and Mark Veraar
summary:
We study stochastic, parabolic-parabolic Keller--Segel equations on the $d$-dimensional torus in scaling critical Besov spaces, for $d \geq 3$. Using stochastic maximal regularity estimates, we prove local well-posedness of the equation, i.e., that there exists a unique solution up to a maximal time of existence. We show that the time of existence can be made arbitrarily large with arbitrarily high probability, provided that the initial data is sufficiently small in these critical spaces.
  Contribution to the Oberwolfach Report for the Seminar 'Stochastic Partial Differential Equations in Critical Spaces' organized by Antonio Agresti and Mark Veraar.

AI.tldr: The paper proves local well-posedness for stochastic parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel equations on the d-dimensional torus (d≥3) in scaling critical Besov spaces, using stochastic maximal regularity estimates. It further shows that the maximal time of existence can be made arbitrarily large with high probability when initial data is sufficiently small in these critical spaces.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to establish well-posedness results for stochastic Keller-Segel equations in critical Besov spaces, extending existing deterministic theory to the stochastic setting and addressing the challenge of critical-space analysis for this parabolic-parabolic system in dimensions d≥3.
AI.method: The approach relies on stochastic maximal regularity estimates to handle the stochastic parabolic system in scaling critical Besov spaces on the torus, enabling a local well-posedness argument with a maximal time of existence.
AI.result: Local well-posedness is established: a unique solution exists up to a maximal time. Additionally, arbitrarily large existence times are achievable with arbitrarily high probability for sufficiently small initial data in the critical Besov spaces.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that the stochastic Keller-Segel system is well-posed in critical Besov spaces, with a probabilistic stability guarantee for small initial data ensuring long-time existence with high probability.

title: Volume Stability for Hyperbolic Manifolds and Applications to General Relativity
summary:
We prove a sharp volume-stability theorem for closed hyperbolic three-manifolds. Let \((M,h)\) be closed hyperbolic with \(\operatorname{Ric}_h=-2h\), and let \(g_i\) be smooth metrics on \(M\) satisfying $R(g_i)\geq -6, \operatorname{Vol}_{g_i}(M)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Vol}_h(M)$. After passing to a subsequence, there exist \(Z_i\subset M\), smooth domains \(K_i\subset M\), and diffeomorphisms $ψ_i:K_i\longrightarrow M\setminus Z_i $
such that $\operatorname{Vol}_{g_i}(Z_i)\longrightarrow0, \operatorname{Vol}_h(M\setminus K_i)\longrightarrow0, $
and $
\|ψ_i^*g_i-h\|_{C^0(K_i,h)}\longrightarrow0. $
Thus near-equality in the sharp hyperbolic volume bound forces tensorial \(C^0\)-convergence to the hyperbolic metric outside regions of vanishing volume. As an application, we establish stability of the Fischer--Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian at the Lorentz-cone ground state: after CMC normalization, near-minimizing compact vacuum data in the hyperbolic topological class converge, modulo sets of vanishing volume, to the hyperbolic Lorentz-cone geometry in tensorial \(C^0\). This provides a rigorous volume-dominance formulation of the Fischer--Moncrief asymptotic picture.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a sharp volume-stability theorem for closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds: metrics with scalar curvature bounded below by -6 and volume approaching the hyperbolic volume must converge in tensorial C^0 to the hyperbolic metric outside vanishing-volume regions. This is applied to establish stability of the Fischer-Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian, showing near-minimizing vacuum data converge to the hyperbolic Lorentz-cone geometry.
AI.motivation: To understand the rigidity and stability of hyperbolic volume bounds in dimension three, and to rigorously establish the Fischer-Moncrief asymptotic picture for compact vacuum spacetimes near the Lorentz-cone ground state.
AI.method: The authors prove a sharp volume-stability theorem via a compactness/contradiction argument: they show that for any sequence of metrics satisfying R(g_i) >= -6 with volumes approaching the hyperbolic volume, they can extract subsequences, find smooth domains K_i and diffeomorphisms to M minus small exceptional sets Z_i, and establish C^0 convergence of the pulled-back metrics to the hyperbolic metric on these large domains. They then apply this geometric stability result to the Fischer-Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian setting, after imposing a CMC normalization on compact vacuum data.
AI.result: The sharp volume-stability theorem holds: near-equality in the hyperbolic volume bound forces tensorial C^0-convergence to the hyperbolic metric outside regions of vanishing volume (Vol(Z_i) -> 0, Vol_h(M\K_i) -> 0). As an application, stability of the Fischer-Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian at the Lorentz-cone ground state is established, providing a rigorous volume-dominance formulation of the Fischer-Moncrief asymptotic picture.
AI.conclusion: The volume-stability theorem provides a sharp quantitative rigidity statement for hyperbolic 3-manifolds under scalar curvature bounds, and its application to the Fischer-Moncrief Hamiltonian establishes a rigorous stability result for compact vacuum spacetimes in the hyperbolic topological class, confirming the Lorentz-cone ground state as the volume-dominant geometric limit.

title: On convolved weight matrices and local solvability with controlled loss of regularity
summary: We introduce the convolution between abstractly given anisotropic weight matrices and investigate properties of this new construction. Further, we apply the knowledge to the particular but interesting case when the (isotropic) matrices are associated with weight functions in the sense of Braun-Meise-Taylor and show how the convolution of associated weight matrices modifies the underlying weight functions. Finally, we give a concrete application of the convolution when studying the concept of local solvability for a certain hyperbolic PDE. Indeed, the convolution allows to treat in a natural way a mixed setting; i.e. having a controlled loss of regularity expressed in terms of two, in general different, weight sequences.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a convolution operation for abstract anisotropic weight matrices, analyzes its properties, applies it to weight functions in the Braun-Meise-Taylor sense to see how it affects underlying weight functions, and demonstrates a concrete application to local solvability of a hyperbolic PDE where the convolution naturally handles mixed settings with two different weight sequences controlling regularity loss.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to develop a new mathematical construction (convolution of weight matrices) that can naturally handle mixed regularity settings, particularly in the context of PDE solvability where different weight sequences may control different aspects of regularity loss.
AI.method: The paper defines a convolution operation for abstract anisotropic weight matrices, studies its properties, then specializes to the case where isotropic matrices come from Braun-Meise-Taylor weight functions to understand how the convolution modifies the underlying weight functions.
AI.result: The convolution construction is developed and its properties are established, with demonstrated application to local solvability of a hyperbolic PDE, showing that the convolution naturally handles a mixed setting with potentially different weight sequences controlling regularity loss.
AI.conclusion: The convolution of weight matrices provides a natural framework for treating mixed regularity loss scenarios in PDE analysis, particularly for hyperbolic local solvability problems.

title: Well-posedness and large deviations for the obstacle problem of first-order stochastic conservation laws
summary: This paper studies the obstacle problem for first-order scalar conservation laws driven by multiplicative noise. By adapting a barrier-substitution strategy to the kinetic formulation, we permit the reflection measure to be a general Radon measure and eliminate the usual obstacle-noise compatibility condition. We establish the existence of kinetic solutions for continuous obstacles and further derive $L^1$-contraction and uniqueness under stronger spatial regularity. Moreover, we prove a Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle in $L^1(0,T;L^1(\mathbb{T}^N))$. Unlike existing large-deviation arguments based on control-uniform penalization of the obstacle, we work directly with the reflected skeleton equation and retain the possibly singular Radon reflection measure throughout, while a viscous approximation provides the spatial $H^1$-regularity required for compactness before passing to the inviscid limit. Our results provide a hyperbolic counterpart to the large deviation theory for parabolic reflected SPDEs developed by Matoussi, Sabbagh, and Zhang (2021).

AI.tldr: The paper studies the obstacle problem for first-order scalar conservation laws with multiplicative noise. By adapting a barrier-substitution strategy to the kinetic formulation, they allow general Radon measures as reflection measures, eliminating the usual obstacle-noise compatibility condition. title: Reflected diffusion, no-flux continuity equations and confined Lagrangian flows in bounded domains
summary: Motivated by marginal distribution flows of reflected diffusions in bounded domains, we investigate when a density/flux pair solving a no-flux continuity equation admits a regular Lagrangian flow that remains in the closed domain and generates the prescribed density flow. We give sufficient conditions in terms of interior bounded-variation regularity, bounded-variation control on a boundary collar, a one-sided bound on an absolutely continuous divergence, and vanishing normal trace of the velocity. The proof uses the fact that tangency removes the singular boundary contribution to the divergence of the zero extension, thereby making the extended velocity admissible for the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory. We show that these boundary assumptions cannot be jointly relaxed so as to admit a boundary current mechanism. We construct an explicit smooth density/flux pair carrying a boundary current. Its density evolution is unique in a weighted class and its characteristics are unique, confined and transport the marginals, yet it admits no regular Lagrangian flow because the compressibility bound fails arbitrarily close to the initial time. We also establish two uniqueness results for no-flux Fokker-Planck equations: a duality result for bounded measurable drifts and a weighted energy result for entrance-type drifts singular at the boundary. Our results provide a rigorous mathematical justification for using the ODE-based sampling of reflected diffusion models under minimal regularity assumptions on the coefficients, and also indicate when such ODE-based samplers may fail.
